2027-06-06.title: Third Sunday after Pentecost
readings: The Twelve sent out two by two
We will not worship the golden statue
Through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed
I am the bread of life
2027-06-06.verse: I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty.
theo: Jesus says: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never be hungry, and whoever believes in me will never be thirsty… Anyone who comes to me I will never drive away… This is indeed the will of my Father, that all who see the Son and believe in him may have eternal life; and I will raise them up on the last day.” And: “No one can come to me unless drawn by the Father who sent me.” Faith itself is a gift: the Father draws, the Spirit moves the heart.

In the evening Gospel Jesus is rejected in his own town: “Prophets are not without honor, except in their hometown, and among their own kin, and in their own house.” Yet he does not stop. He sends the Twelve two by two, with authority over unclean spirits. “So they went out and proclaimed that all should repent. They cast out many demons, and anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them.” The mission of the Church begins in weakness and is carried by the Spirit's power.

In the book of Daniel three young men stand before a golden statue and a blazing furnace. They say to the king: “If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the furnace of blazing fire and out of your hand, O king, let him deliver us. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods and we will not worship the golden statue that you have set up.” This is faith that does not bargain: God first, whatever happens.

St Paul writes: “So then, whenever we have an opportunity, let us work for the good of all, and especially for those of the family of faith… May I never boast of anything except the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ… a new creation is everything!” In Baptism we became a new creation; the bread of life keeps us alive as God's new people.
conn: Joseph's brothers.
Genesis 42: the brothers recognise their guilt; Jeremiah 3: “Return to me”; Acts 13:38: forgiveness proclaimed through Jesus.
The furnace.
Daniel 3: fidelity under threat; Galatians 6:14: boasting only in the Cross.
Anointing with oil.
Mark 6:13: the apostles anoint the sick; the Church sees here a hint of the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (James 5:14).
Bread in Egypt.
Joseph gives grain to his hungry brothers (Genesis 42:25); Jesus is the bread of life for the world.
altar: “I am the bread of life.” At the Holy Qurbono the Father draws us to the Son, and the Son gives himself to us, so that we may never hunger and may be raised on the last day.
outline: Opening
Rejected at home, yet sending others.
Point 1 · The bread of life
Come to Jesus; he will never drive you away.
Point 2 · Sent two by two
Mission in weakness: repentance, healing, anointing.
Point 3 · But if not
The three young men: faith without bargaining.
Point 4 · A new creation
Doing good to all, boasting only in the Cross.
Take-home line
“Anyone who comes to me I will never drive away.”
live: Go two by two
Visit a sick or lonely person this week with a family member or friend.
Faith without bargaining
Tell God: “Even if you do not answer as I wish, I will trust you.”
Receive worthily
Prepare for Holy Qurbono with confession if needed.
fathers: St Augustine
“No one comes unless drawn.” You are drawn not by force but by delight; show a green branch to a sheep and you draw it; so Christ, revealed by the Father, draws us (Tractates on John 26, 4–5).
St Hippolytus of Rome
The three youths teach us that the faithful must prefer death to denying God, and God stood with them in the furnace (Commentary on Daniel II).
magis: Catechism 1406
“I am the living bread that came down from heaven; whoever eats of this bread will live for ever.”
Catechism 1511
The Church believes that a special sacrament for the sick was instituted by Christ, hinted at in Mark 6:13 and promulgated by James 5:14.
Catechism 2087–2089
Faith requires us to worship God alone and refuse all idols.
saints: 8 June: St Mariam Thresia. 11 June: Mar Barthulmai (Bartholomew) and Mar Barnabas, Apostles; anniversary of the erection of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Hierarchy (11 June 1932). 13 June: St Antony of Padua.
2027-06-06.prayer: Lord Jesus, bread of life, draw us to yourself and never drive us away. Make us faithful like the three young men in the furnace, send us two by two to heal and proclaim repentance, and make us a new creation for the good of all. Amen.

2027-06-20.title: Fifth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: Whoever wants to be first must be servant of all
Three times a year you shall keep a festival
I will be like the dew to Israel
Those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength
Ananias and Saul: a chosen instrument
We are the temple of the living God
You give them something to eat
2027-06-20.alt: Season of Pentecost. The Apostles' Fast (Sleehanombu) is under way, ending on 29 June.
2027-06-20.verse: Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.
theo: In the Gospel the crowd is hungry and the day is ending. The disciples want to send them away. Jesus says: “You give them something to eat.” They have only five loaves and two fish. Jesus “taking the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowd. And all ate and were filled.” What little we bring, Christ blesses and multiplies; but he gives it through the hands of his disciples. This is the priesthood: hands that receive from Christ and give to the people.

In the evening Gospel the disciples argue about who is the greatest. Jesus sits down, calls the Twelve and says: “Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.” Then he takes a little child in his arms: “Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.” The Church does not need ambitious men but servants.

In Acts the Lord sends Ananias to Saul, the persecutor: “Go, for he is an instrument whom I have chosen to bring my name before Gentiles and kings and before the people of Israel.” Ananias lays hands on him, and Saul is filled with the Holy Spirit. God calls unexpected people, and he uses other people's hands to form them. Seminaries exist for this: so that those whom God chooses may be formed to serve.

Isaiah encourages the weary: “He gives power to the faint… those who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary.” Priests and seminarians, catechists and parents grow tired. The Spirit renews those who wait on the Lord.
conn: Bread in the wilderness.
The feeding of the five thousand recalls the manna and points to the Eucharist: “blessed and broke them, and gave them to the disciples.”
Festival and first fruits.
Exodus 23: Israel offers the first fruits; the Church offers her sons and daughters to God's service.
Chosen instrument.
Acts 9:15: Saul the persecutor becomes Paul the apostle.
Temple of the living God.
2 Corinthians 6:16: we are God's temple; holiness of life is the soil of vocations.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the priest does what the disciples did: he receives the bread blessed and broken by Christ and gives it to the people. Pray today for priests and for those preparing to be priests.
outline: Opening
Five loaves, two fish, and a hungry crowd.
Point 1 · You give them something to eat
Christ feeds through his disciples.
Point 2 · Servant of all
True greatness in the Church.
Point 3 · A chosen instrument
God calls and forms: Ananias, Saul, the seminary.
Point 4 · Wings like eagles
Renewed strength for those who serve.
Take-home line
“Whoever wants to be first must be servant of all.”
live: Pray for a seminarian
Pray each day this week for the seminarians of your eparchy, by name if you know one.
Bring your five loaves
Offer your time or talent to your parish, however small.
Serve without being seen
Do one service at home that no one asks for.
fathers: St Ambrose
He gave the loaves to the disciples to distribute, as he gives the Bread of heaven through the ministry of the Church (Exposition of Luke 6, 84–86).
St Gregory the Great
The pastor must be a servant first; he who seeks to rule rather than to serve is not a shepherd (Pastoral Rule I).
magis: Catechism 1335
The miracles of the multiplication of the loaves prefigure the superabundance of the Eucharist.
Catechism 1548
In the ministry of the priest it is Christ himself who is present to his Church as Head and Shepherd.
Optatam Totius 2
The duty of fostering vocations falls on the whole Christian community, especially families.
saints: 24 June: Birth of St John the Baptist. 29 June (Tue): Sts Peter and Paul, end of the Apostles' Fast.
2027-06-20.prayer: Lord Jesus, you took the five loaves, blessed and broke them, and gave them to your disciples for the crowd. Bless our seminarians and priests; make them servants of all; renew the strength of all who are weary in your service, and send labourers into your harvest. Amen.

2027-06-27.title: Sixth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: Increase our faith; we are worthless slaves
Some take pride in chariots, but our pride is in the name of the Lord
Paul at the Areopagus: in him we live and move
2027-06-27.alt: Season of Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today Seminary Day, with the collection for the Major Seminary, and the memory of Yakob Mar Theophilos (1956). Family Day and the Seventy-two Disciples come next Sunday, 4 July. The Apostles' Fast ends on Tuesday 29 June (Sts Peter and Paul).
2027-06-27.verse: Just so, I tell you, there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance.
theo: Jesus tells of a shepherd with a hundred sheep who loses one. He leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the lost one “until he finds it. When he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders and rejoices.” And he calls his friends: “Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.” God is not a cold judge counting sins; he is a shepherd who searches and carries. “There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.”

St Paul tells the Corinthians that the Church is a body: “For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ… If one member suffers, all suffer together with it; if one member is honoured, all rejoice together with it.” The family is the first place where we learn this: every member matters, the weakest most of all.

In the evening Gospel Jesus says hard things about forgiveness: “If the same person sins against you seven times a day, and turns back to you seven times and says, ‘I repent,’ you must forgive.” The apostles cry out: “Increase our faith!” Forgiving again and again needs faith that God is greater than our hurt. And Jesus adds: when you have done everything, say, “We are worthless slaves; we have done only what we ought to have done.” No pride, only humble service.

At the Areopagus Paul tells the philosophers of Athens about the unknown God: “he is not far from each one of us. For ‘In him we live and move and have our being.’” God is near every person, searching for them like the shepherd. Our homes should be places where the lost are welcomed back and where God's nearness is felt.
conn: The shepherd king.
2 Samuel 3: Israel is brought together under David the shepherd; Christ the Good Shepherd gathers the lost.
Incense.
Exodus 30: the holy incense rises before God; in the Qurbono incense rises with our prayers and the prayers of the Church.
The Lord's name.
Psalm 20:7: “our pride is in the name of the LORD our God”; Luke 17:10: we are only servants.
One body.
1 Corinthians 12 and Luke 15: no one in the body or the flock is expendable.
altar: The incense that rises at the Holy Qurbono recalls the holy incense of Exodus 30 and the prayers of the saints (Revelation 8:4). Christ the Shepherd, who carried the lost sheep, carries us to the Father in this sacrifice.
outline: Opening
One lost sheep matters.
Point 1 · The shepherd who searches
Joy in heaven over one sinner.
Point 2 · One body
Every member counts, especially the weak.
Point 3 · Forgive seven times
“Increase our faith!”
Point 4 · He is not far
In him we live and move.
Take-home line
“Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.”
live: Bring back one
Call or visit someone in your family or parish who has drifted from the Church.
Family prayer
Pray together as a family every evening this week, even briefly.
Forgive again
Forgive one repeated hurt and ask for more faith.
fathers: St Gregory the Great
The shepherd lays the sheep on his shoulders, for Christ took our human nature upon himself and carried our sins (Homilies on the Gospels 34).
St John Chrysostom
Make your house a church; let the father and mother be like priests teaching the household (Homilies on Genesis 2, 4).
magis: Catechism 1443
Jesus' welcome of sinners shows the reconciliation of the sinner with God and the Church.
Catechism 1655–1657
The Christian family is a domestic church, where the faith is first proclaimed.
Catechism 791
The unity of the Mystical Body: when one member suffers, all suffer.
saints: 29 June (Tue): Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles; Holy Qurbono for the people; end of the Apostles' Fast. 3 July (Sat): Dukrono of St Thomas the Apostle.
2027-06-27.prayer: Good Shepherd, you leave the ninety-nine to seek the one who is lost. Seek us when we stray and carry us home on your shoulders. Make our families one body in you, increase our faith to forgive again and again, and let heaven rejoice over every sinner who returns. Amen.

2027-06-29.title: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles
readings: You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church
Daniel resolves not to defile himself
I have called you by name, you are mine
An angel frees Peter from prison
I have fought the good fight
2027-06-29.alt: Feast of Sts Peter and Paul: Holy Qurbono for the people. End of the Apostles' Fast (Sleehanombu).
2027-06-29.verse: And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it.
theo: At Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answers: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replies: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” The Church rests on the faith Peter confessed and on the office Christ gave him, continued in the Bishop of Rome.

After the Resurrection, by the lake, Jesus asks Peter three times: “Simon son of John, do you love me?” Three times Peter had denied him; three times he now confesses his love; three times Jesus entrusts him: “Feed my lambs… Tend my sheep… Feed my sheep.” Peter's authority is born from mercy and love, and it ends in martyrdom: “someone else will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not wish to go.”

Paul writes from prison near the end of his life: “I am already being poured out as a libation, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.” The persecutor became the apostle of the nations; the fisherman became the rock. Both gave their lives in Rome under Nero, and the Church of Rome is built on their blood.

In Acts, Peter sleeps in prison between two soldiers, and “the church prayed fervently to God for him.” An angel comes, the chains fall from his hands. Today we pray for Peter's successor, Pope Leo XIV, and for our Major Archbishop, in communion with him. The Syro-Malankara Church entered this communion in 1930 precisely to be united with the see of Peter.
conn: Abram called.
Genesis 12: Abram leaves his land at God's word; Peter leaves his nets, Paul his former life.
Called by name.
Isaiah 43:1: “I have called you by name, you are mine”; Simon receives a new name, Peter; Saul becomes Paul.
Daniel's fidelity.
Daniel 1: faithful in a foreign court; Peter and Paul faithful unto death in Rome.
The keys.
Isaiah 22:22: the key of the house of David; Matthew 16:19: the keys of the kingdom.
altar: In every Holy Qurbono of our Church the Pope of Rome is commemorated in the diptychs together with our Major Archbishop and bishop: a sign that we offer the one sacrifice in communion with Peter.
outline: Opening
Two very different men, one faith, one martyrdom.
Point 1 · You are Peter
The rock and the keys: the ministry of unity.
Point 2 · Do you love me?
Authority born of mercy.
Point 3 · I have kept the faith
Paul's race finished.
Point 4 · The Church prayed for him
Our prayer for the Pope and our bishops.
Take-home line
“Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”
live: Pray for the Pope
Pray an Our Father and Hail Mary for Pope Leo XIV and our Major Archbishop today.
Answer Jesus
Tell Jesus three times in prayer: “Lord, you know that I love you.”
Keep the faith
Ask Sts Peter and Paul for courage to keep the faith in a hard situation.
fathers: St Augustine
One day is kept for the passion of both apostles, but they were one; though they suffered on different days, they were one (Sermon 295).
St Leo the Great
Peter and Paul are the two eyes of the body whose head is Christ; through them the Gospel shone on Rome (Sermon 82).
magis: Catechism 881–882
The Lord made Simon alone the rock of his Church; the Pope, Peter's successor, is the perpetual and visible source of unity.
Catechism 553
The power of the keys: authority to govern the house of God.
Lumen Gentium 22
The college of bishops with Peter's successor as its head.
saints: 3 July (Sat): Dukrono of St Thomas the Apostle; Holy Qurbono for the people.
2027-06-29.prayer: Lord Jesus, you built your Church on the rock of Peter's faith and spread your Gospel through Paul's labours. By their prayers keep us faithful to the end; protect Pope Leo, our Major Archbishop and our bishops; and give us hearts that answer you each day: “Lord, you know that I love you.” Amen.

2027-06-13.title: Fourth Sunday after Pentecost
readings: The Lord sends out the seventy
Moses blesses the tribes of Israel
The Lord has given you the city
Who may abide in your tent?
There is a blessing in the cluster
Seven men full of the Spirit and of wisdom
Rejoice that your names are written in heaven
2027-06-13.alt: Season of Pentecost. St Antony of Padua. The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) runs from Wednesday 16 June to Tuesday 29 June, the feast of Sts Peter and Paul: remind the faithful today.
2027-06-13.verse: Nevertheless, do not rejoice at this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.
theo: In the evening Gospel the Lord appoints seventy others and sends them ahead of him in pairs to every town he means to visit. Before he gives them any instruction about what to do, he tells them what to pray for: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.” Mission begins on our knees. The harvest belongs to the Lord, and so do the laborers.

Then comes a strange commission: “See, I am sending you out like lambs into the midst of wolves.” No purse, no bag, no sandals. They are to enter a house and say first, “Peace to this house!” They heal the sick and announce that the kingdom of God has come near. The messenger carries so little so that the message may be seen clearly: the power is God's, not ours. And the Lord binds himself to these poor messengers: “Whoever listens to you listens to me.”

In the Gospel of the Qurbono the seventy come back full of joy: “Lord, in your name even the demons submit to us!” Jesus answers, “I watched Satan fall from heaven like a flash of lightning.” Yet he turns their joy to a deeper source: do not rejoice that spirits submit to you, “but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Success in ministry passes; belonging to God remains. A catechist, a choir member, a priest, a parent who prays with the children: the deepest joy of each is not what they achieve but that God knows them by name.

The other readings fill out the picture. At Jericho the walls fall not by siege engines but by obedience, procession and the sound of the priests' trumpets: “the LORD has given you the city.” In Acts the apostles hand the daily service of the tables to seven men “full of the Spirit and of wisdom” so that they may give themselves to prayer and to serving the word, and “the word of God continued to spread.” St Paul reminds the Corinthians that the cup we bless and the bread we break are a sharing in the Blood and Body of Christ; because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. The Church is sent out from the altar.
conn: Seventy or seventy-two?

Ancient manuscripts of Luke differ: some read seventy, some seventy-two (the NRSV prints seventy, the POC seventy-two). In Genesis 10 the nations of the earth number seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek: the mission of the seventy points to all the nations.
Moses' last blessing.

Deuteronomy 33 is Moses' farewell blessing on the tribes before his death. It ends: “Happy are you, O Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by the LORD.” The seventy are sent to share that blessing with every town.
Seven times round Jericho.

Joshua 6: the priests carry the ark and blow the trumpets; on the seventh day, after the seventh circuit, the walls fall. The victory belongs to the Lord, as the seventy learn when the demons submit “in your name”.
A blessing in the cluster.
Isaiah 65:8: as the vinedresser spares a cluster because there is still good wine in it, God spares his servants. The Lord of the harvest sees what is good in a people before he sees what is wrong.
altar: “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a sharing in the body of Christ?” At the end of the Holy Qurbono we are sent out, as the seventy were, to carry the peace we have received at the altar into our houses and streets.
outline: Opening
Pray before you go: the harvest is the Lord's.
Point 1 · Ask the Lord of the harvest
Vocations begin with prayer.
Point 2 · Lambs among wolves
Peace to this house; the power is God's.
Point 3 · Servants of the word and of the table
The seven in Acts; every ministry in the parish.
Point 4 · Rejoice that your names are written in heaven
The deepest joy is belonging to God.
Take-home line
“Rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”
live: Pray for laborers
Each day this week pray for one priest, one religious and one young person who may be called (Luke 10:2).
Say “Peace to this house”
When you enter a home this week, bless it silently with the words of Luke 10:5.
Prepare for the Apostles' Fast
Decide today how you will keep the Shleeha Nombu from 16 June (Acts 6:4: prayer and the word).
fathers: St Gregory the Great
The world is full of priests, he lamented, yet in God's harvest a true laborer is rarely found; we take up the office but do not do its work (Homilies on the Gospels 17).
St Augustine
Speaking of 1 Corinthians 10:17 to the newly baptised: be what you see, and receive what you are, the Body of Christ (Sermon 272).
magis: Catechism 1396
The unity of the Mystical Body: the Eucharist makes the Church (quoting 1 Corinthians 10:16–17).
Catechism 849–851
The missionary mandate: the Church is sent by Christ to all nations, urged on by the love of God.
Evangelii Gaudium 120 (Pope Francis)
Every baptised person is a missionary disciple; we no longer say that we are “disciples” and “missionaries”, but always “missionary disciples”.
saints: 13 June: St Antony of Padua. 14 June: the prophet Elisha. 15 June: memory of the first church built in honour of the Mother of God. 16 June (Wed): the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins. 18 June: Mar Aprem Malpan (St Ephrem). 19 June: Mar Jude Thaddeus, Apostle.
2027-06-13.prayer: Lord of the harvest, you sent the seventy ahead of you in poverty and peace. Send laborers into your harvest today: priests, religious, catechists and families who announce your kingdom. Make us one body through the one bread we share, give us your peace to carry into every house, and let our deepest joy be that our names are written in heaven. Amen.

2027-06-01.title: Tuesday of the second week after Pentecost · St Justin
readings: The household of God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth; the great mystery of our religion
“When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he”
2027-06-01.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Justin, philosopher and martyr (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56). June, the month of Hziran in the Syriac calendar, opens; in Kerala the schools reopen and the monsoon rains arrive in these days.
2027-06-01.verse: Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.
theo: June begins, and in Kerala it begins with two familiar sounds: the first heavy rain of the monsoon on the roof, and children in new uniforms walking back to school with umbrellas bigger than themselves. It is a month of beginnings, and the Church gives us on its first day a saint who spent half his life searching and the other half teaching: St Justin, philosopher and martyr. In the Epistle St Paul writes to his young co-worker Timothy, who has been left in charge of the Church at Ephesus: “I am writing these instructions to you so that, if I am delayed, you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.” Paul does not call the Church a club of the like-minded or an office that hands out certificates. She is a household, with a Father, brothers and sisters, and a table. And she is a pillar and a bulwark: a pillar holds something up so that it can be seen; a bulwark protects it so that it cannot be knocked down. What the Church holds up and protects is not her own opinion but the truth that God has revealed.

Then Paul breaks into what may be one of the oldest hymns of the Church, sung perhaps in Ephesus before he wrote it down: “Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great: He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among Gentiles, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.” Six short lines tell the whole story of Christ: the Word made flesh, his life and death, his Resurrection shown to be true by the Spirit, the angels at the empty tomb, the apostles going out to the nations, the faith of the peoples, and the Ascension. We have just walked through all of this from Christmas to Pentecost. The “mystery” here is not a riddle that cannot be solved; it is a secret that God has now opened. St Justin was a man who had looked for that secret in every school of his time. Born in Samaria about the year 100, he went from teacher to teacher: a Stoic who did not think it necessary to know God, a Peripatetic who asked first about his fee, a Pythagorean who wanted music and geometry before anything else, a Platonist whose ideas pleased him for a while. Then, as he tells us himself, an old man he met walking by the sea told him to read the prophets, who had spoken of Christ long before he came. “A fire was kindled in my soul,” Justin writes, and he found in Christ the only philosophy that is sure and profitable (Dialogue with Trypho 8, in substance).

In the Gospel the question that Justin had been asking all his life is put to Jesus directly: “Who are you?” Jesus does not answer with a definition. He points to the Cross: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own, but I speak these things as the Father instructed me.” “I am he” echoes the name God gave to Moses at the burning bush. It will be on the Cross, lifted up between earth and heaven, that Jesus shows most clearly who he is: the Son who does always what pleases the Father, and who loves to the end. Justin understood this with his life. He opened a school in Rome, wore the philosopher's cloak to the end, wrote two Apologies to the emperors defending the Christians, and the Dialogue with Trypho, a long and courteous conversation with a Jewish teacher about the Scriptures they both revered. About the year 165 he was arrested with six companions and brought before the prefect Rusticus. Asked to sacrifice to the gods, they answered that they wished for nothing more than to suffer for our Lord Jesus Christ and so be saved (Acts of the Martyrdom of St Justin, in substance). They were beheaded. The man who had searched for the truth in books gave his life for the Truth who is a person. On this first day of June, when students go back to their desks, ask St Justin to teach us to love learning and to seek in it the One who is the Truth.
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I really searching for in my studies, my work and my reading?
Point 1 · The household of God
The Church is a home and a pillar that holds up the truth for all to see.
Point 2 · The great mystery
Six lines that tell the whole story of Christ.
Point 3 · “Who are you?”
Jesus shows who he is on the Cross; St Justin found him and died for him.
Take-home line
“Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great.”
live: Behave as one of the household (1 Timothy 3:15)
Speak of the Church today as you would speak of your own family: honestly, but never with contempt.
Look at the One lifted up (John 8:28)
Before you begin your study or work today, look for a moment at a crucifix and say: Lord, you are he.
2027-06-01.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, revealed in flesh and taken up in glory, you are the truth that St Justin sought in every school and found at last in the Scriptures and in your Cross. Keep your Church faithful as the pillar and bulwark of the truth, and keep us faithful as members of your household. Bless the children and young people who return to school in these days, and their teachers. Give us a mind that loves to learn and a heart that is ready, like St Justin, to confess you before all. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: St Justin wrote, around the year 155, the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist that we have: the readings, the homily, the prayers, the kiss of peace, the bread and the cup brought to the one who presides, the great thanksgiving, and the people's Amen. He said this food is not received as common bread and common drink, but as the flesh and blood of the incarnate Jesus. Every Holy Qurbono is that same gathering.
conn: A hymn and a question.
1 Timothy 3:16 sings who Christ is; in John 8:25 his hearers ask him “Who are you?” The Church's hymn is the answer to the crowd's question.
The Sunday ahead.
On the Third Sunday after Pentecost (6 June) the Church will hear Jesus say “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35); St Justin is the great early witness to that bread on the Christian Sunday.
fathers: St Justin Martyr

The food we call Eucharist is received not as common bread and common drink: as Jesus Christ our Saviour was made flesh by the word of God, so the food over which thanksgiving has been made by the prayer of his word is the flesh and blood of that same Jesus (First Apology 66, in substance).
St Irenaeus
The Church, though spread throughout the world, keeps the one faith she received from the apostles as carefully as if she lived in one house (Against Heresies I.10, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1345

The Catechism quotes at length St Justin's account of the Sunday Eucharist, written to the pagan emperor Antoninus Pius about the year 155, to show that the basic shape of the Eucharistic celebration has stayed the same through the centuries.
Fides et Ratio 38
St John Paul II names St Justin among the Fathers who, having searched in philosophy, found in Christianity the only sure and profitable philosophy, and who kept a high regard for reason.

2027-06-02.title: Wednesday of the second week after Pentecost
readings: The message about the cross: foolishness to some, the power of God to us
The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed and like yeast
2027-06-02.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56).
2027-06-02.verse: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
theo: In the first week of June the farmers of Kerala watch the sky. When the monsoon breaks, they plant: paddy seedlings in the flooded fields, pepper cuttings at the foot of the trees, tapioca stems in the wet red earth. Nothing looks less impressive than a stick pushed into mud. Yet a few months later there is a harvest. Today's readings speak of God's way of working, which is very like the farmer's in June: small, hidden, apparently foolish, and in the end astonishingly fruitful. St Paul begins with the hardest example of all: “For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” To the educated people of Corinth, a city proud of its orators and its schools, a crucified Jew from Galilee was not a message of salvation but a scandal. The cross was the punishment for slaves and rebels, a thing one did not mention in polite company. And Paul builds everything on it.

He knows the objections and names them: “For Jews demand signs and Greeks desire wisdom, but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are the called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Paul is himself a Jew, and he is not mocking anyone; he is describing two honest human hungers, the hunger for a mighty deed and the hunger for a convincing argument, and saying that God has answered both in a way no one expected. The sign is the Son of God dying out of love; the wisdom is the plan of the Father to save the world through weakness. “For God's foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God's weakness is stronger than human strength.” St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, marvelled that twelve unlettered fishermen, armed only with the message of a crucified man, had persuaded the cities and the philosophers of the world; he said that this itself was the greatest proof that the Cross is the power of God (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 4, in substance). We who make the sign of the Cross so easily, on our foreheads, over our food, over our children at night, should remember what a bold thing it is: we are signing ourselves with God's foolishness and declaring that it is wiser than anything the world can offer.

In the Gospel Jesus gives two small pictures of the same truth. “What is the kingdom of God like? And to what should I compare it? It is like a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in the garden; it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.” And again: “It is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.” The mustard seed was proverbial among the Jews for smallness. Three measures of flour was a very large amount, enough to feed a whole household and its guests, and a little yeast, hidden inside it, changes all of it. Neither the seed nor the yeast makes any noise. Both work from within and both take time. This is how the Holy Spirit, poured out at Pentecost, works in the Church and in each of us: through a word of Scripture that stays in the heart, through a Holy Qurbono attended faithfully on an ordinary weekday, through a small act of kindness that nobody sees. We grow impatient and want quick results, big crowds, visible success. The Lord asks us to plant and to knead, and to trust him for the growth. As the rains come down on the fields this week, let us ask him to let the seed of his word fall into our hearts and to let the yeast of the Gospel work quietly through our homes and our parish.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I trust small and hidden things to be the way God works?
Point 1 · The foolishness of the cross
What the world calls weakness is the power of God.
Point 2 · The mustard seed
The smallest beginning becomes a tree with room for the birds.
Point 3 · The yeast in the flour
The Gospel works quietly from within until all is changed.
Take-home line
“To us who are being saved it is the power of God.”
live: Sign yourself with the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18)
Make the sign of the Cross slowly and deliberately three times today, remembering that it is the power of God.
Plant one small seed (Luke 13:19)
Do one small, hidden good deed today and tell no one about it.
2027-06-02.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, you are the power of God and the wisdom of God. When the world laughs at the message of your Cross, keep us faithful to it; when we look for great signs and clever words, turn our eyes back to your love poured out for us. Make your kingdom grow in us like the mustard seed and work in us like yeast hidden in the flour. Bless the rains that fall on our fields in these days and the seed that our farmers sow. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the foolishness of the Cross is made present: the one sacrifice of Christ is offered on the altar under the humble signs of bread and wine. Nothing looks smaller than a piece of bread, and nothing is greater than what it becomes.

2027-06-03.title: Thursday of the second week after Pentecost
readings: Those who believe are blessed with Abraham; we receive the promise of the Spirit through faith
The house swept and put in order, and the seven spirits
2027-06-03.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56). The Latin Church remembers today St Charles Lwanga and his companions, the young martyrs of Uganda (1885–1887).
2027-06-03.verse: in order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
theo: Before the monsoon, every Kerala household does a thorough cleaning: the attic is cleared, the drains are opened, the walls are whitewashed, the old things are thrown out. A swept house is a good thing. But today Jesus tells a strange little story about a swept house that ended badly: “When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it wanders through waterless regions looking for a resting place, but not finding any, it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ When it comes, it finds it swept and put in order. Then it goes and brings seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and live there; and the last state of that person is worse than the first.” The house was clean, but it was empty. Nobody had come to live in it. The point is sharp: it is not enough to get rid of evil; the place it leaves must be filled with good. A person who gives up drinking but finds nothing to fill the evenings, a family that stops quarrelling but never learns to pray together, a young man who leaves a bad company but finds no good one: all these are swept houses, and they are in danger.

St Paul's Epistle tells us who must come to live in the swept house. He writes to the Galatians, who had received the Gospel with joy and were now being told that they must also take on the whole Law of Moses to be true children of Abraham. Paul answers by going back to Abraham himself: “so, you see, those who believe are the descendants of Abraham. And the scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, declared the gospel beforehand to Abraham, saying, ‘All the Gentiles shall be blessed in you.’” Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God, long before the Law was given. Paul honours the Law as God's gift; what he insists on is that no one is made right with God by keeping it by his own strength: “Now it is evident that no one is justified before God by the law; for ‘The one who is righteous will live by faith.’” And then he says what Christ has done: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” The one who hung on the tree took on himself everything that stood against us. St Augustine, commenting on this verse, said that Christ took our punishment without taking our guilt, so that by bearing what was ours he might give us what was his (Commentary on Galatians, in substance).

Why did he do it? Paul answers in the last verse, and it is the verse for this season: “in order that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.” The house is swept by the Cross and filled by the Holy Spirit. This is what happened to us at Baptism: the unclean spirit was driven out by the prayers of exorcism and renunciation, and the Holy Spirit came to dwell in us, sealed in the holy Myron. It is what happens every time we make a good confession: the house is swept. And it is why the Church does not leave us there but calls us to the Holy Qurbono, to prayer, to the word of God, to works of mercy, so that the house is not left empty but is lived in. In these weeks after Pentecost, let us ask the Spirit not only to clean us but to move in and stay. A house where the Spirit lives has no room left for seven other spirits.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I have given up something wrong, what have I put in its place?
Point 1 · Children of Abraham by faith
The blessing promised to Abraham comes to all who believe.
Point 2 · Christ became a curse for us
On the tree he took what was ours to give us what is his.
Point 3 · The swept house must not stay empty
The Spirit received through faith must fill the place evil has left.
Take-home line
“So that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.”
live: Fill the empty room (Luke 11:25–26)
If you have recently given up a bad habit, choose one good practice today to put in its place.
Live by faith (Galatians 3:11)
Before every decision today, say quietly: Lord, I trust in you, not in myself.
2027-06-03.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you became a curse for us on the tree so that the blessing of Abraham might come to all the nations and we might receive the promise of the Spirit. Sweep our hearts clean of every evil, and do not leave them empty: fill them with your Holy Spirit, with prayer, with love and with good works. Keep us faithful children of Abraham through faith, and guard us from falling back into what you have set us apart from. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The house swept clean is meant to receive a guest. In the Holy Qurbono the Lord himself comes to dwell in us: we receive his Body and Blood so that our hearts, cleansed by his mercy, may be filled with his life.

2027-06-04.title: Friday of the second week after Pentecost · Memory of Most Rev. Geevarghese Mar Timotheos
readings: Remember your leaders; Jesus suffered outside the city gate; we have an altar
The faithful and wise slave whom the master finds at work
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life”
“No one has greater love than this”
2027-06-04.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Most Rev. Geevarghese Mar Timotheos (2019), with the readings for the memory of a bishop and three alternative Gospels; these are the only readings printed for the day. It also notes that the Latin Church celebrates today the solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus. First Friday of the month (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56).
2027-06-04.verse: Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured.
theo: Three remembrances meet on this first Friday of June. The Panchangam asks us to remember Most Rev. Geevarghese Mar Timotheos, a bishop of our Church who went to the Lord in 2019. It notes that the Latin Church celebrates today the solemnity of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, and June has long been kept by Catholics of every rite in Kerala as the month of the Sacred Heart. And it is the First Friday, when many of our families go to confession and receive Holy Communion in reparation and love. The readings chosen for the memory of a bishop gather all three together. The Letter to the Hebrews begins: “Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” We remember a bishop not only with gratitude for what he did, but with a prayer that the Lord who called him may receive him, and with a resolve to imitate what was Christlike in him. The memory of a shepherd always sends us back to the Shepherd whose heart was the source of his.

The letter then says something remarkable: “We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.” The Christian altar is not a table of ordinary food; it is the place where the one sacrifice of Christ is made present. And where was that sacrifice offered? “Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured.” Outside the gate, on the hill of Calvary, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and blood and water flowed out. That pierced side is what the Church contemplates in the devotion to the Sacred Heart: not a sentimental picture but the wound through which we see the love of God made flesh. St Bonaventure wrote that his side was pierced so that, through the visible wound, we might see the invisible wound of love (The Tree of Life, in substance). Hebrews draws the practical conclusion: “Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.” Praise and sharing: this is how a heart that has been loved answers.

The Gospel shows the same love in the shape of a steward's faithfulness: “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time? Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.” A bishop is such a steward; so is a priest, a parent, a teacher, a nurse on night duty. The wicked servant thinks “My master is delayed” and begins to treat others as he pleases. The faithful one keeps feeding the household, because he knows whose household it is. The alternative Gospels printed today show the heart of the Master who appoints the stewards: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” “No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends.” On this First Friday, let us thank God for the shepherds who fed us with his word and his Body, pray for the soul of Mar Timotheos, and bring our own hearts to the pierced Heart of Christ, so that they may become a little more like his: gentle, humble, faithful, and ready to share.
outline: Opening
Ask: whose faith have I received, and whose faith am I handing on?
Point 1 · Remember your leaders
A bishop's memory sends us back to the Shepherd's heart.
Point 2 · Outside the gate
The pierced side, the altar, and the sacrifice of praise and sharing.
Point 3 · The faithful steward
Feeding the household on time, because it is the Master's household.
Take-home line
“Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.”
live: Imitate their faith (Hebrews 13:7)
Pray today for the bishop who confirmed you or the priest who baptized you, living or departed, and for the soul of Mar Timotheos.
Do good and share (Hebrews 13:16)
Keep this First Friday by sharing something you have with someone in need, as an offering of love to the Heart of Jesus.
2027-06-04.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, good shepherd, whose side was pierced outside the city gate so that blood and water might flow for the life of the world, we remember today your servant, Most Rev. Geevarghese Mar Timotheos, whom you called to shepherd your people. Grant him rest and light in your presence. On this First Friday we bring our hearts to your Heart: make them gentle and humble like yours, faithful in the tasks you have given us, and generous in praise and in sharing. Give your Church shepherds after your own heart. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: “We have an altar.” Every Holy Qurbono stands at the foot of the Cross outside the city gate: the Body given and the Blood poured out from the pierced side are offered and received. The First Friday Communion is a return of love to the Heart that loved first.
conn: The bishops' readings.
Hebrews 13:7–16 and Matthew 24:45–51 are the readings the Panchangam gives for the memory of a bishop; the alternative Gospels (John 10, 14 and 15) show the heart of the Good Shepherd.
A heart pierced outside the gate.
Hebrews 13:12 speaks of Jesus suffering outside the city gate; John 19:34 tells of the soldier who pierced his side there. The Latin solemnity of the Sacred Heart today reads John 19:31–37.
fathers: St Bonaventure
His side was pierced by the spear so that through the visible wound we might see the invisible wound of love, and enter into his heart (The Tree of Life, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

From his side came water and blood, the symbols of Baptism and of the holy mysteries: from these the Church is born, as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam (Baptismal Catecheses 3, in substance).
magis: Catechism 478

Jesus knew and loved us each and all during his life, his agony and his Passion, and gave himself up for each one of us. He has loved us all with a human heart; for this reason the Sacred Heart of Jesus, pierced by our sins and for our salvation, is rightly considered the chief sign and symbol of that love.
Pope Francis, Dilexit Nos (2024)

In his encyclical on the human and divine love of the Heart of Jesus, Pope Francis invites the Church to rediscover in the pierced Heart of Christ the source of her mission and of a love that reaches out to the wounded world.

2027-06-05.title: Saturday of the second week after Pentecost · St Boniface
readings: From childhood you have known the sacred writings; all scripture is inspired by God
“David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?”
2027-06-05.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Second Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Boniface, bishop and martyr, the apostle of the Germans (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56). On this Saturday the Latin Church also honours the Immaculate Heart of the Blessed Virgin Mary. 5 June is World Environment Day.
2027-06-05.verse: All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that everyone who belongs to God may be proficient, equipped for every good work.
theo: St Paul's second letter to Timothy is the letter of an old man in prison who knows that his end is near. He writes to his son in the faith not about himself but about what must be handed on. “Now you have observed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions, and my suffering the things that happened to me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra.” Timothy had seen it all at close range. Paul does not hide the cost: “Indeed, all who want to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.” Then he points to the two things that will keep Timothy steady when he himself is gone: the people from whom he learned the faith, and the Scriptures he has known since he was a child. “But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it, and how from childhood you have known the sacred writings that are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Timothy learned the Scriptures on the knees of his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Many of us learned them in the same way: a grandmother reading the Bible aloud in the evening by the oil lamp, a mother teaching the first prayers, a Sunday school teacher who made the stories come alive.

Then comes one of the great sentences about the Bible: “All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that everyone who belongs to God may be proficient, equipped for every good work.” The word Paul uses means “God-breathed”. The same breath that gave life to Adam and that the risen Christ breathed on the apostles is in the words of Scripture. That is why the Church reads them in every Holy Qurbono, carries the Gospel book in procession, and kisses it. The Gospel today shows Jesus himself reading Scripture with authority. He quotes Psalm 110: “David himself, by the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son?” The Messiah is David's son by birth, and yet David calls him Lord: he is more than a king of David's line; he is the Son of God, seated at the Father's right hand. Mark adds: “And the large crowd was listening to him with delight.” The word of God, opened by Christ, is not a burden but a joy.

St Boniface, whom the Panchangam remembers today, lived this love of Scripture to the end. Born in Wessex in England about 675 and named Wynfrith, he became a monk and a teacher of the Bible, and he could have stayed in his monastery all his life. But he heard the call to bring the Gospel to the Germanic peoples. Pope Gregory II sent him in 719 and gave him the name Boniface. He preached, baptized, founded monasteries and dioceses, and became the archbishop of the German lands. In old age he went back once more to Frisia, the land where he had first tried to preach. On 5 June 754, at Dokkum, a band of armed men attacked him and his companions as they waited to confirm the newly baptized. Boniface told his companions not to fight. An ancient tradition says that he raised a book of the Gospels over his head as the sword came down. In a letter he once wrote that the Church is like a great ship tossed on the sea, and that the shepherd must not abandon it but keep it on its course (Letter to Cuthbert, in substance). On this Saturday the Latin Church also honours the Immaculate Heart of Mary, who “treasured all these things in her heart”. Like Timothy's mother and grandmother, like Boniface, the Mother of God teaches us to keep God's word in our hearts and to hand it on.
outline: Opening
Ask: from whom did I learn the faith, and to whom am I handing it on?
Point 1 · Continue in what you have learned
The people and the Scriptures that formed us from childhood.
Point 2 · All scripture is God-breathed
The word that teaches, corrects and equips us for every good work.
Point 3 · David's son and David's Lord
Jesus opens the Scriptures; St Boniface died with the Gospel in his hands.
Take-home line
“All scripture is inspired by God.”
live: Continue in what you have learned (2 Timothy 3:14)
Thank God today by name for the person who first taught you to pray or read the Bible.
Equipped for every good work (2 Timothy 3:17)
Read one chapter of a Gospel today, slowly, and choose one good work it asks of you.
2027-06-05.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of David and Lord of David, seated at the right hand of the Father, you opened the Scriptures to the crowds, and they listened with delight. Give us that same delight in your word. Bless the grandparents, parents and teachers who hand on the faith to children, and keep us faithful to what we have learned. Through the prayers of St Boniface, who carried your Gospel to the nations and gave his life holding it, make us bold to proclaim your word in season and out of season. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: In the Holy Qurbono the Gospel book is carried with candles and incense, because in it Christ himself speaks. The God-breathed word prepares the way for the Word made flesh, who gives himself to us on the altar.
conn: The Scriptures and Christ.
2 Timothy 3:15 says the Scriptures instruct us for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus; in Mark 12:35–37 Christ himself shows that Psalm 110 speaks of him.
A Saturday with Mary.
The Latin Church keeps the Immaculate Heart of Mary on this Saturday, with the Gospel of Luke 2:41–51, where the Mother of God “treasured all these things in her heart”.
fathers: St Jerome
Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ (Commentary on Isaiah, Prologue).
St Boniface

The Church is like a great ship sailing on the sea of this world, struck by the waves of trials; we must not abandon it but steer it, not be silent watchers or hirelings who run from the wolf, but watchful shepherds (Letter to Cuthbert, in substance).
magis: Dei Verbum 11

Holy Mother Church holds that the books of both the Old and the New Testament, in their entirety, are sacred and canonical, because, written under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, they have God as their author and teach firmly, faithfully and without error the truth which God wanted put into the sacred writings for the sake of our salvation.
Catechism 133

The Church forcefully and specifically exhorts all the Christian faithful to learn the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ by frequent reading of the divine Scriptures, for ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

2027-06-07.title: Monday of the third week after Pentecost
readings: Lifting up holy hands without anger; adorned with good works
The Advocate will teach you everything; “Peace I leave with you”
2027-06-07.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam (Panchangam 2026–27, p. 56).
2027-06-07.verse: Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.
theo: Yesterday, on the Third Sunday after Pentecost, we heard Jesus send out the Twelve two by two, and say “I am the bread of life.” Today, at the beginning of a new week, the readings turn to the inner life of the community he sends: how it prays, how its members bear themselves, and what gift holds it together. St Paul writes to Timothy: “I desire, then, that in every place the men should pray, lifting up holy hands without anger or argument.” Lifting up the hands was the ancient posture of prayer, and it is still the priest's posture at the altar in our Holy Qurbono, as he stands facing the east with the people behind him. But Paul adds a condition: the hands must be holy, and the heart must be without anger and quarrelling. A man who has just shouted at his wife, a member of a parish committee who has come straight from an argument, cannot lift up holy hands until he has made peace. Jesus said the same: leave your gift at the altar and first be reconciled to your brother. That is why, before the great prayer of offering, the peace is passed from the altar to the people, hand to hand, in every Holy Qurbono.

Paul then turns to the women of the community, asking them to dress “modestly and decently in suitable clothing, not with their hair braided, or with gold, pearls, or expensive clothes, but with good works, as is proper for women who profess reverence for God.” In a Kerala of gold-laden weddings and competitive display, the word is not out of date, and it is addressed to men as much as to women: what makes a Christian beautiful is not what one wears but what one does. The verses that follow are among the hardest in the New Testament for modern ears: “Let a woman learn in silence with full submission. I permit no woman to teach or to have authority over a man.” The Church reads them within the whole of Scripture and her living tradition. Paul is writing about a particular community in Ephesus, troubled by false teachers who had found a hearing in some households (1 Timothy 1:3–7; 2 Timothy 3:6–7), and about order in its public worship. He is not denying what Scripture says from its first page: “So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” Man and woman are equal in dignity (Catechism 369). The Church keeps the apostolic order by which the sacred ministry of priests, the preaching of the homily at the Qurbono among them, is entrusted to ordained men; and she has always rejoiced in women who teach the faith: mothers and grandmothers, catechists, religious sisters, and women Doctors of the Church such as St Catherine of Siena, St Teresa of Avila and St Thérèse of Lisieux. Paul's last line, that the woman “will be saved through childbearing”, was read by some ancient interpreters as pointing to the one Childbirth through which salvation came to all: the Son born of the Virgin Mary, the new Eve.

The Gospel gives the key to reading every hard page: the Holy Spirit. “I have said these things to you while I am still with you. But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything, and remind you of all that I have said to you.” The Spirit poured out at Pentecost is the Church's teacher and memory: he guides her to understand the Scriptures as a whole, without tearing out one verse against another. And the gift the Spirit brings is peace: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled, and do not let them be afraid.” The world gives peace as a truce between enemies, a quiet that lasts until the next quarrel. Christ gives peace as a share in his own life with the Father, a peace that holds even in trouble. St Augustine said that Christ leaves us peace in this world, so that we may overcome the enemy, and will give us his own peace in the world to come, where there will be no enemy left (Tractates on John 77, in substance). This Monday morning, before work and school, let us lift up holy hands, let go of yesterday's anger, and receive the peace that the world cannot give.
outline: Opening
Ask: with what hands and what heart do I come to pray?
Point 1 · Holy hands without anger
Prayer and reconciliation go together; the peace passed at the Qurbono.
Point 2 · Adorned with good works
Beauty in deeds, not display; the hard verses read in the light of all Scripture.
Point 3 · The Advocate and the peace of Christ
The Spirit teaches and reminds; Christ gives a peace the world cannot give.
Take-home line
“Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.”
live: Without anger or argument (1 Timothy 2:8)
Before you pray tonight, make peace with anyone you quarrelled with today, even with a short message.
Receive his peace (John 14:27)
When you feel anxious today, stop and say slowly: Jesus, your peace I receive; I will not be afraid.
2027-06-07.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, before you returned to the Father you left us your peace and promised the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, to teach us everything and remind us of all you said. Take away from our hearts anger and quarrelling, so that we may lift up holy hands in prayer. Clothe us, men and women alike, not with the display of the world but with good works. Let your Spirit lead your Church into all the truth, and let your peace keep our hearts from fear. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Before the anaphora in the Holy Qurbono the peace is given from the altar and passed from hand to hand among the people. We cannot lift up holy hands to receive the Body of Christ while holding anger against a brother or sister; the peace of Christ prepares us for Christ himself.

2027-06-08.title: Tuesday of the third week after Pentecost · St Mariam Thresia
readings: A person is justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ
The Spirit of truth will testify on my behalf; you also are to testify
2027-06-08.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Mariam Thresia (1876–1926), virgin, of Puthenchira, foundress of the Congregation of the Holy Family.
2027-06-08.verse: You also are to testify because you have been with me from the beginning.
theo: The Epistle today takes us into one of the sharpest moments of the early Church. At Antioch, Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, and then, when visitors came from Jerusalem, he drew back, as if the table of Christ had two classes of guests. Paul opposed him to his face, and in today's verses he gives the reason: “We ourselves are Jews by birth and not Gentile sinners; yet we know that a person is justified not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. And we have come to believe in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by doing the works of the law, because no one will be justified by the works of the law.” Paul is not speaking against good works, nor against the law God gave to Israel. He is saying that no one, Jew or Gentile, can stand before God by a record of achievements. We are made righteous because Christ has loved us and given himself for us, and we receive that gift by faith. That is why the table cannot be divided: everyone who sits there sits by the same grace. In the Holy Qurbono the priest and the newest catechumen, the old family and the migrant worker, come forward with the same empty hands.

Then Paul adds a warning: “But if I build up again the very things that I once tore down, then I demonstrate that I am a transgressor.” He means the walls that Christ pulled down between people, and the old self-reliance that grace pulled down in us. It is possible to be set right by God and then quietly to begin building again: to start keeping accounts of our virtues, to look down on those who pray less or give less, to think that our place at the altar is earned. The Christian life is not a building of our own that God inspects at the end; it is a life received. St Augustine put his whole experience of grace into one short prayer: give what you command, and then command what you will (Confessions 10.29, in substance). Everything good we do is first his gift, and our part is to receive it and not to block it.

The Gospel comes from the Last Supper. Jesus promises: “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, he will testify on my behalf. You also are to testify because you have been with me from the beginning.” There are two witnesses here, the Spirit and the disciples, and they speak together. The Spirit does not testify instead of us; he testifies through us, in our words and our lives. Today the Church remembers one in whom that double witness was very plain: St Mariam Thresia of Puthenchira, near Thrissur. Born in 1876, she gave herself from childhood to prayer, and as a young woman she went with a few companions to the homes of the sick, the dying and the poor, and to families torn by quarrels and debts, without asking which church or which community they belonged to. In 1914 she founded the Congregation of the Holy Family to carry on this work, and she died on 8 June 1926. Pope Francis canonized her on 13 October 2019. She was a daughter of the Syro-Malabar Church, and our Panchangam keeps her memory with gladness, for the saints belong to the whole Church. Her works were many, but she never thought she had earned anything by them: she was simply letting the Spirit testify to Jesus through her hands. In this month when families settle into a new school year and the monsoon keeps people indoors, she reminds us that the first place of witness is the home.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I live as someone who has received everything, or as someone who is building up a record?
Point 1 · Justified through faith in Jesus Christ
No one stands before God by achievements; the same grace seats all at one table.
Point 2 · Do not build again what grace tore down
The walls between people and the pride of self-reliance.
Point 3 · The Spirit testifies, and you also
St Mariam Thresia: a witness carried into the homes of the poor and the sick.
Take-home line
“You also are to testify because you have been with me from the beginning.”
live: Receive before you give (Galatians 2:16)
Begin each good work today with a short prayer: Lord, this is your gift; let me not spoil it.
Witness at home (John 15:27)
Visit, or at least telephone, one family you know that is going through sickness, debt or a quarrel, and pray with them if they wish.
2027-06-08.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you loved us and gave yourself for us, and by faith in you we are made righteous before the Father. Keep us from building again the walls you have pulled down and the pride you have broken in us. Send us the Spirit of truth, who comes from the Father, to testify to you in our words and our lives. Through the prayers of St Mariam Thresia, who carried your love into the homes of the sick, the poor and the troubled, make our families holy, peaceful and open to all who need us. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar no one is seated by merit: the Body and Blood of Christ are given to sinners made righteous by his love, and from the altar we are sent, like St Mariam Thresia, to carry that love from house to house.
conn: The quarrel at Antioch.

Galatians 2:11–14, just before today's reading, tells how Paul opposed Peter when Peter drew back from eating with Gentile believers; today's verses give the principle behind the dispute: all are justified by faith in Christ.
The two witnesses.

John 15:26–27 promises the Spirit's testimony and the disciples' testimony together; Acts 1:8 shows the promise fulfilled when the Spirit comes and the apostles become witnesses to the ends of the earth.
A saint of the family.
St Mariam Thresia gave her congregation the name of the Holy Family of Nazareth (Luke 2:51–52), and she sent her sisters into homes as the Spirit's witnesses.
fathers: St Augustine
Give what you command, and command what you will: every good work is first God's gift before it is ours (Confessions 10.29, in substance).
St John Chrysostom
When Paul writes “who loved me and gave himself for me”, he teaches each believer to say it personally, as if Christ had died for that one person alone (Commentary on Galatians 2:20, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1987
The grace of the Holy Spirit has the power to justify us, cleansing us from our sins and giving us the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ and through Baptism (in substance).
Catechism 2204
The Christian family is a specific revelation and realization of the communion of the Church, and for this reason it can and should be called a domestic church.
Catechism 1830
The moral life of Christians is sustained by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, permanent dispositions that make us docile in following his promptings.

2027-06-09.title: Wednesday of the third week after Pentecost
readings: They exchanged the truth about God for a lie
“I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?”
2027-06-09.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost.
2027-06-09.verse: I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live
theo: The Epistle today is one of the hardest pages St Paul ever wrote, and it is wise to read it whole, in its place. Paul is beginning his letter to the Romans by showing that the whole human race needs the Gospel. The root of all that goes wrong, he says, is not first a bad deed but a false worship: “they exchanged the truth about God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever! Amen.” When God is pushed out of the centre, something else is put there: pleasure, money, power, the self. And three times Paul repeats a frightening phrase: “God gave them up.” God does not need to send a thunderbolt. He respects our choice and lets us have what we have chosen, and the choice bears its own fruit. A heart that will not acknowledge God slowly loses its sense of what is true and good, in the body, in the mind and in every relationship. St Augustine saw this in his own youth: he had looked for beauty and joy in created things instead of in the One who made them, and found only restlessness (Confessions 10.27, in substance).

Among the fruits of that exchange Paul names sexual acts between persons of the same sex. The Church, faithful to the word of God, teaches that such acts are contrary to the Creator's plan and can never be approved, because the gift of sexuality belongs within the faithful marriage of a man and a woman, open to life (Catechism 2357). But we must not stop reading there, as if this page were about other people. Paul's list goes on: “They were filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, covetousness, malice. Full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, craftiness, they are gossips, slanderers, God-haters, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, rebellious toward parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless.” Gossip, envy, boasting, disobedience to parents: there is no one in the church this morning who is not somewhere on this list. And the very next sentence of the letter, which we do not read today, turns on the reader: “Therefore you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you judge others.” The Catechism asks us to receive every person who carries this struggle with respect, compassion and sensitivity, avoiding every sign of unjust discrimination (Catechism 2358), and it calls every one of us, beginning with ourselves, to chastity and conversion (Catechism 2348, 2359). Paul writes this dark chapter only so that the light of chapter 3 may shine: all have sinned, and all may be justified by God's grace through faith in Christ.

The Gospel brings that light into a house of mourning. Lazarus has been in the tomb four days; Bethany is full of neighbours, “many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them about their brother”, a tender picture of a community that shows up for a funeral, as our Kerala villages still do. Martha goes out to meet Jesus with grief and faith mixed together: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died. But even now I know that God will give you whatever you ask of him.” Jesus answers with one of the greatest sentences in the Gospel: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” And Martha, standing near the tomb, makes a confession as full as Peter's: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” Here is the answer to Romans 1. The human heart that exchanged the Creator for creatures ends in the tomb; but the Creator has come to the tomb in person. Whatever has died in us, whatever we have exchanged and lost, the Lord who stands at Lazarus's grave says to us too: even now. In every Holy Qurbono we pray for our departed, and we receive the One who is the resurrection and the life.
outline: Opening
Ask: what have I put at the centre of my life in the place that belongs to God?
Point 1 · The great exchange
Worshipping the creature rather than the Creator, and the meaning of “God gave them up”.
Point 2 · A list that includes all of us
Gossip, envy and boasting stand beside graver sins; no one may judge.
Point 3 · “Even now”
Martha's faith at the tomb, and Jesus, the resurrection and the life.
Take-home line
“I am the resurrection and the life. Do you believe this?”
live: Put God back in the centre (Romans 1:25)
Name to yourself one created thing, a phone, a habit, an ambition, that has crept into the place of God, and give the first minutes of tomorrow morning to prayer instead.
Say Martha's “even now” (John 11:22)
Bring to Jesus one situation you have given up on, in your family or in yourself, and pray: Lord, even now.
2027-06-09.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the resurrection and the life. Too often we exchange the truth about God for a lie and serve created things rather than the Creator; forgive us, and do not give us up to ourselves. Take from us the sins of the tongue and of the heart, gossip, envy, pride and every disorder of the body, and give us clean hearts. When we stand before the tombs of our hopes and of our loved ones, give us Martha's faith to say: even now. Raise us to new life, and bring our departed into the light of your face. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the Creator gives himself to his creatures: in the Holy Qurbono we receive the risen Lord, the resurrection and the life, and the medicine that heals hearts turned away from God.

2027-06-10.title: Thursday of the third week after Pentecost
readings: Epaphroditus came close to death for the work of Christ: honor such people
When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth
2027-06-10.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost.
2027-06-10.verse: When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth
theo: St Paul's letters are full of names we pass over quickly, and today the Church stops at one of them. Epaphroditus was a member of the little church at Philippi, sent by them to Paul in prison with a gift and with orders to stay and help him. In prison he fell ill, so ill that he nearly died, and when he recovered he was homesick and worried that his people were anxious about him. So Paul sends him home with a letter, and with a testimonial that any of us would treasure: “Still, I think it necessary to send to you Epaphroditus, my brother and co-worker and fellow soldier, your messenger and minister to my need.” Brother, co-worker, fellow soldier: three titles of friendship, labour and struggle. And the word translated “messenger” is the Greek word apostolos: the Philippians had sent him, and he was their apostle to Paul. The Church in her season of Pentecost remembers that the apostolic mission does not belong only to the Twelve; it is carried on by thousands of people whose names never reach a history book.

Paul asks the Philippians for something important: “Welcome him then in the Lord with all joy, and honor such people, because he came close to death for the work of Christ, risking his life to make up for those services that you could not give me.” Honour such people. Every parish is held up by an Epaphroditus or two: the catechism teacher who has given thirty Sunday mornings a year for twenty years, the sacristan who opens the church before dawn, the woman who sits with the sick when no one else will go, the young people who carry chairs and clean the hall.
