In these first weeks of June, when the schools of Kerala reopen in the monsoon rain, we might think also of teachers, bus drivers and cooks in school kitchens who will spend themselves for our children all year. And we may think of the many nurses from our parishes who serve in hospitals far from home, like Epaphroditus, sometimes at real risk to their health. Paul also says something tender: “God had mercy on him, and not only on him but on me also, so that I would not have one sorrow after another.” The great apostle does not pretend to be beyond grief; he thanks God for sparing his friend. St John Chrysostom remarks that Paul is not ashamed to show that he was anxious and would have mourned, because love for the brethren is no weakness in a saint (Homilies on Philippians 9, in substance).

The Gospel takes us back to the Last Supper: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” Jesus is a patient teacher. He does not pour everything into the disciples at once; he knows what they can carry. The Spirit continues his teaching through the whole life of the Church, leading her deeper into the one truth that Jesus is, not adding a new Gospel but opening up the one Gospel: “he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” This is what happens in the councils of the Church, in the prayer of the saints, in the slow growth of a believer's understanding over a lifetime. It happens to each of us too. There are things in our faith we could not bear at fifteen and understand at fifty; there are crosses whose meaning we will see only later. Like a good teacher at the start of a school year, the Spirit begins where we are. Our part is to stay in the classroom: to keep coming to the Holy Qurbono, where the word is read and the Bread of Life is given, and to let him guide us, one step at a time, into all the truth.
outline: Opening
Ask: whom have I never thanked for the hidden service that keeps my parish and my family going?
Point 1 · Brother, co-worker, fellow soldier
Epaphroditus, the Philippians' apostle to Paul, and the unnamed bearers of the mission.
Point 2 · Honour such people
The parish workers, teachers and nurses who spend themselves for others; God's mercy in sickness.
Point 3 · Into all the truth
The patient teaching of the Spirit, who takes what is Christ's and declares it.
Take-home line
“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.”
live: Honour an Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:29)
Write a note, send a message or say a word of thanks this week to one person whose hidden service holds up your parish, school or family.
Stay in the Spirit's classroom (John 16:13)
Choose one question about the faith that troubles you, bring it to prayer before the Holy Qurbono, and ask the Spirit to teach you in his time.
2027-06-10.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you sent your apostles and their co-workers to carry the Gospel, and you send your Spirit of truth to guide your Church into all the truth. We thank you for every Epaphroditus among us, for those who serve without being noticed, for teachers and catechists, for nurses and carers, for those who risk their health for others. Have mercy on them in sickness, as you had mercy on your servant, and spare them one sorrow after another. Teach us patiently, as we are able to bear it, and lead us one step at a time into the fullness of your truth. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The Spirit who guides the Church into all the truth takes what is Christ's and gives it to us: at the altar he makes bread and wine the Body and Blood of the Lord, and makes us one body of brothers, co-workers and fellow soldiers.

2027-06-11.title: Friday of the third week after Pentecost · Mar Barthulmai Shleeha and Mar Barnabas · Foundation Day of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Hierarchy
readings: Justified by faith, we have peace with God; God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit
“We will come to them and make our home with them”
2027-06-11.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers Mar Barthulmai Shleeha (St Bartholomew the Apostle) and Mar Barnabas, and keeps the Foundation Day of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Hierarchy: on 11 June 1932 Pope Pius XI, by the bull Christo Pastorum Principi, erected the Archeparchy of Thiruvananthapuram and the Eparchy of Tiruvalla.
2027-06-11.verse: Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.
theo: Today is a family feast for our Church. On 11 June 1932, Pope Pius XI, by the apostolic constitution Christo Pastorum Principi, erected the hierarchy of the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, with the Archeparchy of Thiruvananthapuram under Archbishop Mar Ivanios and the Eparchy of Tiruvalla under Bishop Mar Theophilos. Less than two years earlier, on 20 September 1930 at Kollam, these two bishops and a small band of companions had made their profession of the Catholic faith and entered full communion with the Bishop of Rome, keeping the venerable West Syriac liturgy of their fathers. They left churches and properties behind; they brought with them the Holy Qurbono, the prayers of Mar Aprem and the faith of the Apostle Thomas. In 1932 the Church gave that small flock a home of its own: bishops, sees, a hierarchy, an ordered life within the one Catholic communion. In 2005 our Church was raised to the rank of a Major Archiepiscopal Church. We thank God today for all of it, and we remember with respect our brothers and sisters of the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Churches, with whom we share the same roots, the same liturgy and the same fathers, praying together for the unity that Christ desires.

The readings the Panchangam gives for this day could hardly be more fitting. St Paul writes: “Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand.” Access and standing: the language of someone who has been brought into a house and given a place in it. And the source of it all is not human planning but divine love: “hope does not disappoint us, because God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.” St Augustine loved this verse above almost any other; he taught that the very love with which we love God is itself God's gift, poured out by the Spirit, so that whatever good we do is grace from beginning to end (On the Spirit and the Letter 5, in substance). Paul goes on to speak of reconciliation: “For if while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more surely, having been reconciled, will we be saved by his life.” The reunion of 1930 was a work of reconciliation, and Mar Ivanios understood it not as a victory over anyone but as a step towards the unity for which Christ prayed. The work is not finished. Every Christian division is a wound in the body of Christ, and the love poured into our hearts asks us to keep praying, to keep speaking kindly, and to keep the door open.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks at the Last Supper of the home that God makes with those who love him: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.” Before this he has promised: “I will not leave you orphaned; I am coming to you,” and he has spoken of “another Advocate, to be with you forever.” A hierarchy is not, in the first place, an organisation chart. It is one of the ways the Lord keeps that promise: through bishops in communion with the successor of Peter, through the sacraments they celebrate and the faith they guard, the Holy Spirit makes sure that the flock is never left orphaned. St Gregory the Great, preaching on this Gospel, said that the proof of love is the display of works: we show that we love by keeping his word (Homilies on the Gospels 30, in substance). Our Church will celebrate this anniversary well, not with speeches only, but by being a home where the Father and the Son are glad to live: faithful to the word, generous to the poor, eager for unity, joyful in the liturgy.

The Panchangam also remembers two apostles today. Mar Barthulmai, St Bartholomew, is one of the Twelve whose names stand in every list of the apostles; many in the tradition identify him with Nathanael, of whom Jesus said: “Here is truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit!” An ancient report preserved by Eusebius says that when the teacher Pantaenus travelled to India, he found Christians there who had a Gospel of Matthew left to them by Bartholomew (Church History 5.10); the tradition of the Churches places his martyrdom in Armenia. Mar Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus, was called by the apostles “son of encouragement”. He sold his field for the poor, he took the newly converted Saul by the hand when everyone else was afraid of him, and he was sent to Antioch, where “the disciples were first called Christians”. It was in that church of Antioch, while they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, that the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” Our liturgy comes to us from the Syriac tradition of Antioch, and next Wednesday we begin the Apostles' Fast. On this day of our Church, Barnabas teaches us to encourage, Bartholomew teaches us to be without deceit, and both teach us that a Church is built on the faith of the apostles.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I treat my Church as an institution I belong to, or as a home where God lives with us?
Point 1 · 1930 and 1932
The reunion at Kollam and the erection of the hierarchy: a home given to a small flock.
Point 2 · Peace, access, reconciliation
Justified by faith, reconciled through the Son, filled with the love the Spirit pours out.
Point 3 · “Not orphaned”
Bishops in communion with Peter's successor as one way the Lord keeps his promise to make his home with us.
Point 4 · Bartholomew and Barnabas
The apostle without deceit and the son of encouragement; Antioch, prayer and fasting.
Take-home line
“We will come to them and make our home with them.”
live: Keep the home open (John 14:23)
Pray today for our Major Archbishop-Catholicos, our bishops and our eparchies, and for one family in your parish that has drifted away.
Be a Barnabas (Acts 4:36)
Speak one word of encouragement this week to someone who is new, struggling or doubted by others.
2027-06-11.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you promised not to leave us orphaned, and in your love you gave our Syro-Malankara Church a home within the one Catholic communion. We thank you for Mar Ivanios, Mar Theophilos and all who walked with them, for the hierarchy erected in 1932, and for all our bishops, priests, religious and faithful. Pour your love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, keep us faithful to your word, and make our Church a home where the Father and you are glad to dwell. Through the prayers of Mar Barthulmai, your apostle without deceit, and of Mar Barnabas, son of encouragement, heal the divisions among your disciples and bring all who call on your name into the unity you desire. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbono celebrated by our bishops and priests in communion with the successor of Peter is the heart of the home the Lord has given us: around one altar the Father and the Son come to make their home with those who love them.
conn: The day of the hierarchy.

Romans 5:1–11 speaks of peace, access and reconciliation; John 14:15–24 of the home God makes with those who love him. On the anniversary of 11 June 1932 both describe what the Church received: an ordered home in the one Catholic communion.
Barnabas at Antioch.

Acts 11:22–26 tells how Barnabas was sent to Antioch, brought Saul there, and how the disciples were first called Christians there; Acts 13:1–3 shows the church of Antioch worshipping and fasting when the Spirit set apart Barnabas and Saul. Our Church's liturgy belongs to the Syriac tradition of Antioch, and the Apostles' Fast begins next Wednesday (16 June).
Bartholomew and Nathanael.
Bartholomew is named in every list of the Twelve (Matthew 10:3; Acts 1:13); many in the tradition identify him with Nathanael of John 1:45–49, the Israelite in whom there is no deceit.
fathers: St Augustine

The love of God poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans 5:5) is not the love by which God loves us only, but the love by which he makes us lovers of him: even our loving is his gift (On the Spirit and the Letter 5 and 32, in substance).
St Gregory the Great
The proof of love is the display of works: whoever says that he loves God and does not keep his word is deceived (Homilies on the Gospels 30, on John 14:23, in substance).
Eusebius of Caesarea

When Pantaenus went as far as India, he found that the Gospel of Matthew had come there before him, left by the apostle Bartholomew (Church History 5.10, in substance; the India of ancient writers may mean lands beyond Arabia).
magis: Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3

The individual Churches, whether of the East or of the West, are of equal dignity; none is superior to the others by reason of its rite, and all enjoy the same rights and obligations under the guidance of the Roman Pontiff (in substance).
Lumen Gentium 23
The particular Churches are formed in the image of the universal Church; in and from them the one and only Catholic Church comes into being.
Ut Unum Sint 54
The Church must breathe with her two lungs, the East and the West, and the treasures of the Eastern traditions belong to the whole Church (in substance).

2027-06-12.title: Saturday of the third week after Pentecost
readings: My heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved
If you have faith the size of a mustard seed, nothing will be impossible for you
2027-06-12.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Third Sunday after Pentecost. Tomorrow, the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost, the faithful are reminded of the Apostles' Fast, which begins on Wednesday 16 June.
2027-06-12.verse: For truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.
theo: The Epistle opens with one of the most moving sentences St Paul ever wrote: “Brothers and sisters, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved.” He is speaking of his own people, the people of Israel. A chapter earlier he has said that he would wish himself cut off from Christ for their sake, and he has listed with pride what belongs to them: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs, and, according to the flesh, the Messiah himself. Paul never stopped being a son of Israel, and he never stopped loving his people. When he says, “I can testify that they have a zeal for God, but it is not enlightened,” he is not sneering; he is remembering his own past, when his zeal had made him a persecutor. The Church has learned from Paul to speak of the Jewish people with reverence and gratitude. The Second Vatican Council, recalling these very chapters of Romans, teaches that the Jews remain most dear to God because of their fathers, for the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Nostra Aetate 4). No Christian may speak of them with contempt.

Then Paul gives the heart of his Gospel: “For, being ignorant of the righteousness that comes from God, and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God's righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.” The word “end” here means both the finishing point and the goal, as the finishing line is the end of a race. Our Malayalam Bible renders it: Christ has fulfilled the law. The whole law was running towards him. This is a warning for us, not for others. It is very possible to be zealous for God and still to be trying to establish our own righteousness: to fast, pray, give and serve as a way of being someone in God's eyes and in the parish's eyes. In a few days we begin the Apostles' Fast. Paul tells us in advance how to keep it: not to establish our own righteousness, but to submit to God's, receiving from Christ what we could never make ourselves.

The Gospel brings us down from the mountain of the Transfiguration into a crowd and a family in distress. A father kneels before Jesus: “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is an epileptic and he suffers terribly; he often falls into the fire and often into the water. And I brought him to your disciples, but they could not cure him.” Every parent who has sat up at night with a sick child, or watched a son or daughter fall into the fire and the water of addiction, depression or bad company, knows this prayer. Jesus heals the boy at once. When the disciples ask privately why they had failed, he answers: “Because of your little faith. For truly I tell you, if you have faith the size of a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.” Many ancient manuscripts add a further verse, printed as a footnote in our English Bible: this kind goes out only by prayer and fasting. Whatever its place in the text, the Church has always heard in this Gospel a call to the faith that prays and fasts. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, remarked that the mustard seed looks small but is the most powerful of seeds; so faith, small to look at, carries the power of God within it (Homilies on Matthew 57, in substance). On this Saturday, let parents bring their children to Jesus by name, and let all of us ask for the small, real faith that moves mountains.
outline: Opening
Ask: for whom is my heart's desire and prayer to God that they may be saved?
Point 1 · Paul's heart for his people
Love, reverence and gratitude for Israel; the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
Point 2 · Zeal without knowledge
Christ is the end of the law; do not establish your own righteousness.
Point 3 · Faith the size of a mustard seed
A father's prayer, the disciples' failure, and the faith that prays and fasts.
Take-home line
“If you have faith the size of a mustard seed … nothing will be impossible for you.”
live: Pray Paul's prayer (Romans 10:1)
Write down the names of three people whose salvation is your heart's desire, and pray for them by name every day of the Apostles' Fast.
Bring your child to Jesus (Matthew 17:15)
Parents and grandparents: tonight, lay your hand on the head of each child or grandchild and pray: Lord, have mercy on my son, on my daughter.
2027-06-12.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the end of the law and the righteousness of all who believe. Give us Paul's heart, full of love and prayer for others, and keep us from every contempt for the people of the covenant, to whom your gifts and calling remain. Take from us the zeal that seeks to establish our own righteousness, and teach us to receive everything from you. Have mercy on our sons and daughters who fall into the fire and the water; heal them and bring them home. Give us faith the size of a mustard seed, and as the Apostles' Fast draws near, teach us to pray and to fast with humble hearts. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The Holy Qurbono is the righteousness of God given, not earned: Christ, the end of the law, offers himself for us, and the smallest faith that receives him receives the power that moves mountains.

2027-06-14.title: Monday of the fourth week after Pentecost · Elisha the Prophet
readings: Present your members to God as instruments of righteousness
None of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian
2027-06-14.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers Elisha the Prophet (Eliša Nbiya). The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins on Wednesday 16 June.
2027-06-14.verse: There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.
theo: Today the Panchangam remembers Elisha the Prophet, and the Gospel names him. Elisha was a farmer's son, ploughing with twelve yoke of oxen, when Elijah passed by and threw his mantle over him; he left the plough, killed the oxen, fed the people with the meat and followed (1 Kings 19:19–21). When Elijah was about to be taken up, Elisha asked for one thing: “Please let me inherit a double share of your spirit.” The Books of Kings then tell of a ministry full of mercy: water made sweet, a poor widow's oil that flowed until every borrowed jar was full, a dead child given back to his mother at Shunem, a hundred people fed with twenty loaves of barley and some left over. Even after his death, a dead man who touched his bones came to life. The Fathers saw in Elisha a figure of Christ, who also fed the crowds, raised the dead and gave his Spirit in full measure to his disciples. Many Eastern Churches keep his memory on this day, and so do we, two days before the Apostles' Fast begins.

In the Gospel Jesus has just read from Isaiah in the synagogue of Nazareth and announced that the Scripture is fulfilled. His neighbours admire him, and then begin to doubt: is this not Joseph's son? Jesus answers with two stories from their own Scriptures: “But the truth is, there were many widows in Israel in the time of Elijah, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, and there was a severe famine over all the land; yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon. There were also many lepers in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian.” A Gentile widow and a Syrian army commander: God's mercy had always reached beyond the borders people drew around it. Origen, preaching on this passage, saw in Naaman a figure of the nations who would be cleansed through the true Elisha, our Lord, in the waters of Baptism (Homilies on Luke 33, in substance). Jesus is not insulting his own people; he is reminding them, as a prophet of Israel, of what Israel's own prophets had already shown. But the truth stings: “When they heard this, all in the synagogue were filled with rage.” They try to throw him from the cliff. “But he passed through the midst of them and went on his way.” No anger can stop the mission of mercy. It will go on, through Galilee to Jerusalem, and through the apostles to the ends of the earth, and to Kerala.

St Paul tells us today how that mercy takes hold of a life: “Therefore, do not let sin exercise dominion in your mortal bodies, to make you obey their passions. No longer present your members to sin as instruments of wickedness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and present your members to God as instruments of righteousness. For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace.” Naaman went down into the Jordan proud and came up clean; we went down into the waters of Baptism and came up from death to life. St Ambrose taught the newly baptised that Naaman was healed not by the water of the Jordan alone but by the word of God and grace working in it, and that the same is true of the font (On the Mysteries 3–4, in substance). But the old habits of the body and the tongue still pull at us; the Catechism calls this the struggle left to us after Baptism, a struggle in which grace gives us the victory (Catechism 1264). On Wednesday the Apostles' Fast begins. It is a time to take back our members from sin and to offer them to God: eyes that look with purity, a tongue that blesses, hands that give, a stomach that learns to say no, feet that go to those in need. Like Elisha, let us ask for a double share of the Spirit, and like Naaman, let us humbly go down into the water of repentance.
outline: Opening
Ask: which part of me, eyes, tongue, hands or appetite, still serves sin rather than God?
Point 1 · Elisha the Prophet
From the plough to the prophet's mantle; a double share of the Spirit and a ministry of mercy.
Point 2 · Naaman the Syrian
God's mercy beyond borders, the anger at Nazareth, and Jesus who passes through the midst of them.
Point 3 · Instruments of righteousness
Baptised from death to life, we offer our members to God: preparing for the Apostles' Fast.
Take-home line
“Present your members to God as instruments of righteousness.”
live: Choose your fast (Romans 6:13)
Before Wednesday, decide on one concrete way to offer your body to God during the Apostles' Fast: a meal, a habit of the eyes or the tongue, an hour of the phone given to prayer.
Go beyond the border (Luke 4:27)
Do one act of kindness this week for someone outside your usual circle of family, caste, community or language.
2027-06-14.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the prophet greater than Elijah and Elisha; your mercy reached the widow of Zarephath and Naaman the Syrian, and it has reached us. In Baptism you brought us from death to life: do not let sin rule in our mortal bodies, but make our members instruments of righteousness. As the Apostles' Fast draws near, give us, as you gave Elisha, a double share of your Spirit, and the humility of Naaman to go down into the waters of repentance. When anger or prejudice rises against your word, pass through the midst of it and carry your mercy on its way. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Elisha fed a hundred with twenty loaves and some were left; at the altar the true Prophet feeds the multitude with his own Body and Blood, and those brought from death to life in Baptism are made his members, instruments of righteousness.
conn: Elisha in the Gospel.
Luke 4:27 recalls 2 Kings 5:1–14, where Naaman the Syrian is healed after washing seven times in the Jordan at Elisha's word; Luke 4:25–26 recalls Elijah and the widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:8–16).
Elisha and Jesus.

2 Kings 4:42–44 (a hundred fed with twenty loaves, with some left over) and 2 Kings 4:32–37 (a dead son given back to his mother) are echoed in the feeding of the crowds and the raising of the widow's son at Nain (Luke 7:11–17).
Baptism and the fast.
Romans 6:3–4 speaks of being buried with Christ in Baptism; today's verses 12–14 draw the moral consequence, which the Apostles' Fast (16–29 June) puts into practice.
fathers: Origen

Naaman the Syrian, cleansed when the lepers of Israel were not, is a figure of the nations cleansed by the spiritual Elisha, our Lord and Saviour, in the mystery of Baptism (Homilies on Luke 33, in substance).
St Ambrose

Naaman doubted when told to wash in the Jordan, yet he was healed; so the newly baptised should believe that it is not the water alone that cleanses, but the grace and power of God working through it (On the Mysteries 3–4, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1264

After Baptism certain consequences of sin remain, among them the inclination to sin that Tradition calls concupiscence; it is left for us to wrestle with, and it cannot harm those who do not consent but resist it manfully by the grace of Jesus Christ (in substance).
Catechism 1434
Interior penance can be expressed in many ways, and Scripture and the Fathers insist above all on three forms: fasting, prayer and almsgiving.
Catechism 2015
The way of perfection passes by way of the Cross; there is no holiness without renunciation and spiritual battle.

2027-06-15.title: Memory of the first church built in the name of the Mother of God · Tuesday of the fourth week after Pentecost
readings: In whatever condition you were called, there remain with God
The true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth
2027-06-15.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam keeps the memory of the founding of the first church in the name of the holy Mother of God; it does not say where or when that church was built. The Apostles' Fast begins tomorrow.
2027-06-15.verse: But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such as these to worship him.
theo: Today the Panchangam asks us to remember the founding of the first church built in the name of the holy Mother of God. It gives no place and no date, and we do not need to supply them. What it wants us to remember is enough: very early, the disciples of Jesus began to raise houses of prayer and to give them the name of his Mother. Think how many churches in our own villages and towns are called St Mary's, Marth Mariam, the church of the Mother of God. Every one of them is a grandchild of that first church. And the Gospel the Church gives us for this memory is, surprisingly, a word of Jesus about the place of worship. At the well of Sychar the Samaritan woman raises the old dispute between her people and the Jews: is God to be worshipped on this mountain or in Jerusalem? Jesus answers: “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” He does not despise the faith of Israel; he says plainly that “salvation is from the Jews.” But he announces something new: “the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such as these to worship him.”

Does this mean that church buildings no longer matter? Not at all. Worship “in spirit and truth” does not mean a vague prayer anywhere and nowhere. The Spirit is the Holy Spirit poured out at Pentecost, and the Truth is Christ himself, who says to the woman, “I am he, the one who is speaking to you.” True worship is worship offered in Christ and through the Spirit, and that happens above all when the Body of Christ gathers around the altar. Solomon knew that no house could hold God: “Even heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you, much less this house that I have built!” A church is not a box for God; it is a home for his people, a sign on earth of the Father's house. St Augustine, preaching on this Gospel, said: if you want to pray in a temple, pray within yourself, but first become a temple of God (Tractates on John 15, in substance). That is why a church is fitting for the Mother of God. She was the first temple of the new covenant, the one in whom the Word dwelt for nine months. St Cyril of Alexandria, preaching at Ephesus in 431, greeted her as the Mother of God, the temple that cannot be destroyed, holding him whom no place can hold (Homily at Ephesus, in substance). A church that bears her name does not compete with her Son; like her at Cana it says, “Do whatever he tells you.”

The Epistle brings the lesson home. The Christians of Corinth were tempted to think that holiness meant changing their circumstances: the circumcised wanted to hide it, the uncircumcised wanted to be circumcised, the married wondered whether to separate. Paul says: stop looking elsewhere. “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing; but obeying the commandments of God is everything.” And again: “In whatever condition you were called, brothers and sisters, there remain with God.” God is to be worshipped in spirit and truth in the church, and then in the kitchen, the paddy field, the shop, the office and the classroom that has just reopened after the summer. The holy Mother of God herself lived for years in an ordinary house at Nazareth, cooking, drawing water and keeping the words of God in her heart. Her first sanctuary was a home. So today, thank God for the church where you were baptised, and then make your own house and work a place where the Father finds a true worshipper.
outline: Opening
Ask: when I come to church, do I bring my whole life with me, or only an hour?
Point 1 · In spirit and truth
Jesus at the well: the Father seeks worshippers in the Spirit and in Christ, the Truth.
Point 2 · A house named for the Mother of God
Churches are homes for God's people, not boxes for God; Mary was the first temple of the Word.
Point 3 · Remain with God where you were called
Worship continues at home and at work, as it did in the house of Nazareth.
Take-home line
“In whatever condition you were called, brothers and sisters, there remain with God.”
live: Worship in spirit and truth (John 4:23)
Come ten minutes early to the next Holy Qurbono and spend them in silence before the altar, asking the Holy Spirit to make your worship true.
Remain with God (1 Corinthians 7:24)
Begin the ordinary work of today with a short prayer offering it to God, and end it with thanks.
2027-06-15.prayer: Father in heaven, you seek true worshippers who will worship you in spirit and truth. Pour your Holy Spirit on us, who gather in houses of prayer built in your name and in the name of the holy Mother of God. As she welcomed your Word and became his first dwelling, let us welcome him in the Holy Qurbono and carry him into our homes and our work. Wherever you have called us, keep us with you, faithful to your commandments and glad in your service. Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with you and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Every church is built for its altar: there, in the Holy Qurbono, the Word who once dwelt in the womb of the holy Virgin comes to dwell among us under the forms of bread and wine, and we become the worshippers the Father seeks.
conn: The woman at the well.
John 4:21–26 is the heart of the conversation at Jacob's well; before it Jesus offers living water (John 4:10–14), and after it many in the town believe (John 4:39–42).
A house too small for God.
1 Kings 8:27: Solomon confesses that the temple cannot contain God; the church building is a sign of his presence among his people, not a container.
The first dwelling of the Word.
John 1:14 and Luke 1:35: the Word became flesh in the womb of the Virgin; the Council of Ephesus (431) confessed her as Mother of God.
fathers: St Augustine
If you wish to pray in a temple, pray within yourself; but first become a temple of God, for he hears in his temple the one who prays (Tractates on John 15, in substance).
St Cyril of Alexandria
Hail, Mary, Mother of God, temple that cannot be destroyed, who held within you the One whom no place can hold (Homily at Ephesus, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1179

The worship in Spirit and truth of the New Covenant is not tied exclusively to one place; but when the faithful gather, they are the living stones built into a spiritual house, and their churches show the Church living in that place.
Catechism 1186
The visible church is a symbol of the Father's house towards which the People of God is journeying, where the Father will wipe every tear from their eyes.
Catechism 495
Called in the Gospels the mother of Jesus, Mary is acclaimed by Elizabeth as the mother of my Lord; the Church confesses that she is truly Mother of God.

2027-06-16.title: The Apostles' Fast begins · Wednesday of the fourth week after Pentecost
readings: Servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries
Jesus gives authority to the Twelve; the names of the twelve apostles
2027-06-16.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. Today the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) begins; it is kept until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June, when the fast ends.
2027-06-16.verse: Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.
theo: Today the Apostles' Fast begins. On Sunday the priests reminded us of it, as the Panchangam asked them to do, and from today until the feast of Sts Peter and Paul the Church keeps it. Why fast now, only a few weeks after the joy of Pentecost? Jesus himself gave the answer when he was asked why his disciples did not fast: “The wedding guests cannot mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them, can they? The days will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then they will fast.” The Bridegroom has ascended to the Father; the Spirit has come; and now the Church, like the apostles, sets out on the long road of mission. The Acts of the Apostles shows how the first Christians did it. At Antioch, “while they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.’” Then, after more fasting and prayer, they laid hands on them and sent them off. The fast of the apostles is a fast for mission: we deny ourselves a little so that the Church may be sent, and so that we ourselves may go where the Spirit sends us. St Leo the Great, preaching in Rome on the fast that followed Pentecost, told his people that after the days of holy rejoicing the Church fasts so that the gifts of the Spirit may be guarded by self-discipline, and he called it a fast handed down from the apostles (Sermons on the Fast of Pentecost, in substance). Our Orthodox brothers and sisters of the Malankara tradition keep this fast too, and it is good to know that in these days many Christians of our land are praying and fasting together.

The Gospel gives the fast its faces. “Then Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to cure every disease and every sickness.” Then Matthew does something he rarely does: he writes out a list of names. “First, Simon, also known as Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee, and his brother John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the one who betrayed him.” These are not titles but persons: two pairs of brothers from the fishing boats of Galilee, a tax collector who had worked for the hated ruling power, and a Simon whose surname probably marked him as a man of zeal, two men who might once have quarrelled bitterly, now seated at one table. Our own Mar Thoma is there, the apostle whom our fathers' faith remembers as the one who brought the Gospel to India. Bartholomew, whom the Panchangam remembered last week, and Thaddaeus, whom it will remember on Saturday, are there too. And the list ends with a name that should make every disciple humble: Judas, chosen like the others, who betrayed. Jesus chose these twelve and gave them his own authority; through them the Church is apostolic. Our bishops are their successors, and our priests share their work. In this fast we pray for them by name.

St Paul tells the Corinthians how to think of the apostles and of all who serve the Church: “Think of us in this way, as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.” A steward manages what belongs to someone else. The mysteries of God, the word, the sacraments, the Holy Qurbono which our tradition loves to call the holy mysteries, do not belong to the priest; he holds them in trust. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, says that a steward does not treat his master's goods as his own, but distributes them faithfully, and so must every servant of the Church (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 10, in substance). And in a smaller way every Christian is a steward: of time, of money, of the body, of the faith received in Baptism. That is what the fast trains us for. When we fast, pray more and give alms, we learn that our food, our hours and our money are not simply ours. Paul adds a warning for the fast: “Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart.” A fast that makes us harsh judges of others, especially of our priests, is no fast at all. Let these days make us trustworthy stewards, slow to judge and quick to pray.
outline: Opening
Ask: what will I give up in these days of the Apostles' Fast, and for whom will I offer it?
Point 1 · A fast for mission
The Bridegroom has gone up; the Church fasts and is sent, as at Antioch.
Point 2 · The Twelve by name
Persons, not titles; Mar Thoma among them; our bishops their successors.
Point 3 · Trustworthy stewards
The mysteries are held in trust; fasting teaches stewardship and forbids rash judgement.
Take-home line
“It is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy.”
live: A fast for mission (Acts 13:2)
Decide today, alone or as a family, on one concrete fast for these days, according to the guidance of our Church, and set aside what it saves for someone in need.
Pray for the apostles of today (Matthew 10:1–4)
Each day of the fast, pray one Our Father for the Pope, one for your bishop and one for your parish priest, by name.
2027-06-16.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you called the Twelve by name, gave them your authority and sent them to proclaim your kingdom. As we begin the Apostles' Fast, strengthen us by your Holy Spirit to deny ourselves for the sake of your Gospel. Make us trustworthy stewards of your mysteries and of all you have entrusted to us. Keep us from judging before the time, and fill your Church with apostles who will carry your word to every nation. Bless our Holy Father the Pope, our bishops and our priests, the successors and helpers of your apostles. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The holy mysteries entrusted to the apostles are placed on our altar in every Holy Qurbono: the priest, a steward and not an owner, offers the one sacrifice of Christ, and a fasting people receives the Bread that strengthens it for mission.
conn: The Bridegroom taken away.
Matthew 9:15: Jesus foretells that his disciples will fast when the Bridegroom is taken from them; the Church's fasts after the Ascension answer that word.
Fasting before sending.
Acts 13:2–3: the Church of Antioch worships and fasts, the Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, and after fasting and prayer they are sent.
A night of prayer before the choice.
Luke 6:12–16: Jesus spends the night in prayer before he chooses the Twelve and names them apostles.
fathers: St Leo the Great

After the days of Pentecost rejoicing, the Church keeps a fast handed down from the apostles, so that the gifts received from the Holy Spirit may be guarded by self-discipline (Sermons on the Fast of Pentecost, in substance).
St John Chrysostom

A steward does not treat the goods of his master as his own but distributes them faithfully; so must everyone who serves in the Church, for what he handles belongs to God (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 10, in substance).
magis: Catechism 1434
The interior penance of the Christian can be expressed in many ways; Scripture and the Fathers insist above all on three forms: fasting, prayer and almsgiving.
Catechism 1438

The seasons and days of penance in the course of the liturgical year are intense moments of the Church's penitential practice, suited to spiritual exercises, voluntary self-denial and fraternal sharing.
Lumen Gentium 20
The bishops, by divine institution, have succeeded to the place of the apostles as shepherds of the Church; whoever hears them hears Christ.

2027-06-17.title: Thursday of the fourth week after Pentecost
readings: Rooted and built up in Christ; the record against us nailed to the cross
The house built on rock and the house without a foundation
2027-06-17.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) is being kept; it ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June.
2027-06-17.verse: As you therefore have received Christ Jesus the Lord, continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
theo: The monsoon has come to Kerala, and with it the yearly lesson of the rivers. We have seen how quickly water rises, how a canal becomes a river and a river becomes a sea, and how some houses stand while others crack and fall. Jesus knew such floods in Galilee, and he uses them in today's Gospel: “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I tell you? I will show you what someone is like who comes to me, hears my words, and acts on them. That one is like a man building a house, who dug deeply and laid the foundation on rock; when a flood arose, the river burst against that house but could not shake it, because it had been well built.” The other man built “on the ground without a foundation,” and “immediately it fell, and great was the ruin of that house.” Notice that both men hear the words of Jesus. Both build. Both houses face the same flood. The difference is hidden underground: one dug deeply, the other did not bother. The difference between them is not hearing but doing. It is possible to call Jesus “Lord, Lord” every Sunday, to sing beautifully in the Qurbono, to know many hymns by heart, and still to be building on sand, because the words we hear never reach the place where we decide how to live.

St Paul uses the same picture, and adds another: “continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.” Rooted like a tree, built up like a house: the Christian life needs both depth and growth. And Paul tells the Colossians why Christ alone can be the foundation: “For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have come to fullness in him.” There were teachers in Colossae offering something more, philosophies, special days, powers of the universe to be feared and placated. Paul answers: you lack nothing in Christ. Then he describes what happened in Baptism, in words our Church sings at every font: “when you were buried with him in baptism, you were also raised with him through faith in the power of God, who raised him from the dead.” And he gives one of the most moving images in all his letters. Our sins were like a written record, a bond of debt signed in our own hand, standing against us. God took that record, “erasing the record that stood against us with its legal demands. He set this aside, nailing it to the cross.” St John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, says that Christ did not merely cancel the bond but tore it in pieces and nailed it up for all to see, as a sign that it could never be used against us again (Homilies on Colossians 6, in substance).

Here is the rock under the house. Not our good resolutions, which are often sand, but what Christ has done: the debt nailed to the cross, the powers disarmed, the new life given in Baptism. Our part is to dig deeply: to let his word go down past our feelings and habits to the place where we choose. The Apostles' Fast, which began yesterday, is a time for digging. When we fast, we feel the ground shift a little; we discover how much of our peace depended on comfort, food, our phone, other people's approval. Underneath, if we keep digging, we find the rock that does not move. In these monsoon days, when you hear the rain on the roof at night, let it remind you to ask: on what is my life built? And pray for those whose houses are threatened by water this season, and for all who have lost homes in floods. A Christian who is rooted in Christ is not spared the floods, but is not swept away by them.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I only hear the words of Jesus, or do I let them reach the decisions of my day?
Point 1 · Two builders, one flood
Both hear, both build, both face the river; only one digs deeply.
Point 2 · Rooted and built up in Christ
In him the fullness of God dwells; nothing is lacking.
Point 3 · The record nailed to the cross
Baptism buried us with Christ; our debt is cancelled and nailed up for all to see.
Take-home line
“Rooted and built up in him and established in the faith.”
live: Dig deeply (Luke 6:48)
Choose one word of Jesus you know well but do not live, and put it into practice today in one concrete act.
Abound in thanksgiving (Colossians 2:7)
Before sleeping tonight, thank God by name for three things he gave you today, including the rain.
2027-06-17.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, in you the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and in you we have come to fullness. You nailed to the cross the record that stood against us and raised us with you in Baptism. Do not let us call you Lord, Lord, and fail to do what you say. Help us in these days of fasting to dig deeply and build our lives on the rock of your word, so that when the floods come we may stand firm. Protect all who are threatened by the waters of this season, and give shelter to those who have lost their homes. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The cross on which our debt was nailed stands over every altar: in the Holy Qurbono the one sacrifice of Calvary is made present, and those who were buried with Christ in Baptism are fed with his risen life.

2027-06-18.title: Friday of the fourth week after Pentecost · Mar Aprem Malpan (St Ephrem the Syrian)
readings: The law has only a shadow of the good things to come
I have called you friends; love one another as I have loved you
2027-06-18.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) is being kept; it ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The Panchangam keeps today the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian, deacon and Doctor of the Church.
2027-06-18.verse: I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father.
theo: Today our Church keeps the memory of Mar Aprem Malpan, St Ephrem the Syrian, the greatest poet of our Syriac tradition. He was born at Nisibis in Mesopotamia at the beginning of the fourth century, served the Church there as a deacon and as a teacher of the faith, and when Nisibis was handed over to Persia in 363 he went with many Christians to Edessa, where he taught and wrote until his death in 373. He never became a priest or a bishop; he remained a deacon, a servant, all his life. Yet his hymns, the madrashe, taught the faith to whole peoples, and they are still sung in the prayers of the Syriac Churches, ours among them. He wrote them for choirs of women and girls, so that the doctrine of the Church might be carried home on melodies that people loved. The Syriac tradition calls him the Harp of the Spirit. In 1920 Pope Benedict XV declared him a Doctor of the universal Church. It is fitting that his memory falls in the Apostles' Fast: Ephrem was a man of fasting and prayer, and tradition remembers that in his last years, when famine struck Edessa, he left his cell to organise help for the hungry and the sick.

The Epistle of the day is a passage Ephrem would have loved. “Since the law has only a shadow of the good things to come and not the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered year after year, make perfect those who approach.” The sacrifices of the old covenant were true worship given by God to Israel, but they were shadows cast ahead by the coming light. “For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.” Only the one offering of Christ does that. Ephrem saw the whole Bible and the whole of creation as full of such shadows and symbols, which our tradition calls raze, mysteries. The lamb, the ark, the manna, the rock in the desert, the dew, the pearl, the olive and its oil: everything, for him, was a window through which Christ could be seen. He wrote that the Word of God is like a living spring: whoever drinks from it takes only a little and leaves far more behind, and should give thanks for what he has received instead of grieving over what he could not take in (Commentary on the Diatessaron 1, in substance). That is how he read Scripture, with wonder and thanksgiving, never pretending to have exhausted it. And Ephrem sang tenderly of the holy Mother of God, through whom the reality came into the world. Addressing Christ, he wrote that only he and his Mother are beautiful in every way, for in him there is no blemish and in his Mother no stain (Nisibene Hymns 27, in substance).

The Gospel shows what the shadows were pointing to: not only a perfect sacrifice but a friendship. “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. No one has greater love than this, to lay down one's life for one's friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you. I do not call you servants any longer, because the servant does not know what the master is doing; but I have called you friends.” The old sacrifices could not make the worshippers perfect; the sacrifice of Christ makes servants into friends. And Jesus adds: “You did not choose me but I chose you. And I appointed you to go and bear fruit, fruit that will last.” Ephrem's fruit has lasted for sixteen centuries; every time the Syriac Churches sing his hymns, the friend of Christ is still bearing fruit. Ours may be smaller and hidden: a prayer taught to a child, a hymn sung with love, a meal given to a hungry neighbour. On this Friday of the fast, let us give thanks for the friendship Christ offers us, and ask Mar Aprem to teach us to sing it.
outline: Opening
Ask: do I relate to God as a servant afraid of his master, or as a friend who knows his heart?
Point 1 · The shadow and the true form
The old sacrifices were shadows; only Christ's offering takes away sin.
Point 2 · Friends, not servants
The sacrifice of the Cross makes servants into friends, and friends love one another.
Point 3 · The Harp of the Spirit
Mar Aprem saw Christ in every symbol of Scripture and creation, and sang the faith.
Take-home line
“I have called you friends.”
live: Read like Mar Aprem (Hebrews 10:1)
Take one Old Testament story you know, such as the manna or the Passover lamb, and ask in prayer how it points to Christ.
Love as he loved (John 15:12)
On this Friday of the fast, give a meal or its cost to someone who is hungry, as Mar Aprem did in the famine of Edessa.
2027-06-18.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, the shadows of the law have passed and you have come, the true and only sacrifice that takes away sin. You no longer call us servants but friends. Through the prayers of Mar Aprem Malpan, the Harp of the Spirit, open our eyes to see you in the Scriptures and in all your creation, teach us to praise you with joy, and make us love one another as you have loved us. Let our lives bear fruit that will last, to the glory of your Father and the Holy Spirit, now and for ever. Amen.
altar: What the sacrifices of the law could only foreshadow is given on our altar: in the Holy Qurbono the one offering of Christ is made present, and the Lord who laid down his life for his friends gives himself to us as food. Mar Aprem sang that in the bread there is hidden fire.
conn: The one sacrifice.
Hebrews 10:5–10, read tomorrow, continues today's passage: Christ comes to do the Father's will, and we are sanctified through the offering of his body once for all.
The vine and its fruit.
John 15:1–10 comes just before today's Gospel: the friends of Jesus bear fruit only by remaining in him, as branches in the vine.
Moses, friend of God.
Exodus 33:11: the Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend; in Christ that friendship is offered to all.
fathers: St Ephrem the Syrian

Who can grasp even one of your words, Lord? We leave behind far more than we take, like the thirsty who drink from a spring; let the one who drinks give thanks and not grieve that the spring is greater than his thirst (Commentary on the Diatessaron 1, in substance).
St Ephrem the Syrian
You alone, Lord, and your Mother are beautiful in every way: in you there is no blemish, and in your Mother no stain (Nisibene Hymns 27, in substance).
magis: Catechism 614

The sacrifice of Christ is unique; it completes and surpasses all other sacrifices. It is first a gift from God the Father himself, and at the same time the offering of the Son who willingly and lovingly gives his life.
Catechism 1158

The beauty of images, music and song serves the Church's prayer; the harmony of signs, song, music, words and actions is more expressive and fruitful when it springs from the cultural richness of the people who pray.
Benedict XVI, General Audience, 28 November 2007
St Ephrem is the most important witness of Syriac-speaking Christianity; he shows that theology can be done in poetry, and that poetry can be a way of praying and teaching the faith (in substance).

2027-06-19.title: Saturday of the fourth week after Pentecost · Mar Yuda Thaddai Shleeha (St Jude the Apostle)
readings: “See, God, I have come to do your will”: sanctified through the offering of the body of Christ
Do not resist an evildoer; go the second mile; love your enemies
2027-06-19.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fourth Sunday after Pentecost. The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) is being kept; it ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The Panchangam remembers today Mar Yuda Thaddai Shleeha, St Jude Thaddaeus, one of the Twelve.
2027-06-19.verse: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,
theo: The Letter to the Hebrews lets us overhear what the Son said as he came into the world. Taking the words of a psalm, he says to the Father: “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body you have prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ‘See, God, I have come to do your will, O God.’” This is the prayer of the Incarnation. The body that the Father prepared was formed in the womb of the Virgin Mary, and from the first moment it was a body offered: a life lived entirely to do the Father's will, from the manger to the Cross. “And it is by God's will that we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.” The animal sacrifices could not reach the heart; what pleases God is a will joined to his. St Augustine wrote that Christ is at once the priest who offers and the offering itself, and that he wished the Church's daily sacrifice to be the sign of this, so that the Church, being his body, learns to offer herself through him (City of God 10, in substance). That is why the Holy Qurbono is not a show we watch but a sacrifice we enter: we bring our bodies, our work and our fasting, and place them with his. On this Saturday of the Apostles' Fast, let your prayer be the same as his: “See, I have come to do your will.”

The Gospel shows what doing the Father's will looks like when someone strikes us. “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’” That old law was not cruel; it was a limit, given to stop revenge from growing larger than the injury. Jesus goes further: “But I say to you, Do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also; and if anyone wants to sue you and take your coat, give your cloak as well; and if anyone forces you to go one mile, go also the second mile.” In his time a soldier could force a civilian to carry his pack for a mile. Jesus says: carry it two. He is not asking us to approve of injustice; when he himself was struck before the high priest, he asked, “why do you strike me?” He is asking us to break the chain of evil by refusing to pay it back in the same coin. And then the summit: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” This is exactly what the body prepared for him did on the Cross, where he prayed for those who crucified him. A fast from food is good; a fast from revenge, from the sharp reply, from the grudge we feed every night, is better still.

Today the Panchangam remembers Mar Yuda Thaddai Shleeha, St Jude, one of the Twelve. Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus; Luke calls him Judas son of James. The Gospel of John remembers one question he asked at the Last Supper: “Lord, how is it that you will reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?” Jesus answered: “Those who love me will keep my word, and my Father will love them, and we will come to them and make our home with them.” Jude wanted a great revelation; Jesus promised a home. Christian tradition remembers him as a preacher of the Gospel in the East and a martyr, and links him with the short Letter of Jude, which urges the faithful to “contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints” and to “keep yourselves in the love of God.” Because his name was so like that of the traitor, he was for centuries less invoked; yet the faithful came to love him as the helper in desperate causes, and in many parishes of Kerala people come to novenas in his honour with burdens that seem hopeless. He teaches us that no question is too bold to bring to Jesus, and no situation too dark for the God who comes to make his home with those who love him.
outline: Opening
Ask: when someone hurts me, do I pay back in the same coin, or do I go the second mile?
Point 1 · A body you have prepared for me
The prayer of the Incarnation: Christ comes to do the Father's will and offers himself once for all.
Point 2 · The second mile
Jesus breaks the chain of revenge: turn the cheek, give the cloak, love the enemy.
Point 3 · Mar Yuda Thaddai
The apostle who asked a question and received the promise of God's indwelling.
Take-home line
“Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.”
live: Pray for one who hurt you (Matthew 5:44)
Name before God one person who has wronged you, and pray for his or her good today, sincerely, even if your feelings do not follow yet.
Bring your hardest intention (John 14:22–23)
Write down the intention that seems most hopeless to you and place it before the Lord, asking the prayers of St Jude.
2027-06-19.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, when you came into the world you said to the Father: see, I have come to do your will; and by the offering of your body once for all you have made us holy. Teach us to join our will to yours, to refuse the way of revenge, to go the second mile and to love even our enemies. Through the prayers of your apostle Mar Yuda Thaddai, who asked how you would reveal yourself, come with the Father and make your home in us. Help all who feel that their cause is hopeless, and keep us in your love. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: The body prepared for the Son and offered once for all is given on our altar: in the Holy Qurbono we receive him who did the Father's will to the end, and we learn to offer ourselves with him, even for those who wrong us.
conn: The shadow and the reality.
Hebrews 10:1–4, read yesterday, said that animal sacrifices could not take away sins; today's passage gives the answer: the obedience of the Son made flesh.
The prayer of the psalm.
Psalm 40:6–8: Hebrews puts these words in the mouth of Christ, Here I am; I delight to do your will, O my God.
Jude's question.
John 14:22–23: Judas (not Iscariot) asks how Jesus will reveal himself; Jesus promises that the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love him.

2027-06-21.title: Monday of the fifth week after Pentecost · St Aloysius Gonzaga
readings: Slaves of sin or slaves of righteousness: the end is eternal life
Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all
2027-06-21.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost. The Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu) is being kept; it ends with the feast of Sts Peter and Paul on 29 June. The Panchangam remembers today St Aloysius Gonzaga, religious, patron of young people.
2027-06-21.verse: Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.
theo: Yesterday, on the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost, the evening Gospel already brought us to this house in Capernaum; today the Church lets us stay there a little longer. Jesus has just told the disciples a second time that he will be betrayed, killed and raised. On the road behind him they have been talking about something else. “And when he was in the house he asked them, ‘What were you arguing about on the way?’ But they were silent, for on the way they had argued with one another who was the greatest.” Their silence says everything: they knew the argument would not bear the light of his question. Jesus does not scold them at length. “He sat down, called the twelve, and said to them, ‘Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.’” Then he does something unforgettable. “He took a little child and put it among them; and taking it in his arms, he said to them, ‘Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes not me but the one who sent me.’” In that world a child had no rank, no voice and no claim. Jesus puts the one who counts least in the centre and says: here you will find me, and in me the Father. St Bede, commenting on this scene, says that the Lord set a child before them so that they might learn humility from its simplicity, a child who does not cling to anger or envy (Commentary on Mark, in substance).

St Paul asks the Romans the question that lies under the disciples' argument: whom do you serve? “Do you not know that if you present yourselves to anyone as obedient slaves, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin, which leads to death, or of obedience, which leads to righteousness?” There is no neutral ground. The disciples who wanted to be greatest were, without knowing it, serving pride. Every human life is given to something: money, pleasure, reputation, a career, a political party, or God. Paul says: “just as you once presented your members as slaves to impurity and to greater and greater iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness for sanctification.” Eyes, hands, tongue, time: all can be given either way. And he names the end of each road: “For the wages of sin is death,” but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. Wages are earned; a gift is received. The service of sin pays exactly what it promises, and it promises death. The service of God gives far more than we could earn. The Apostles' Fast, now in its second week, is a time to look at our members, our eyes and our hands and our evenings, and ask honestly whom they are serving.

Today we remember St Aloysius Gonzaga, a young man who answered that question early. He was born in 1568 in northern Italy, the eldest son of a marquis, trained from childhood for power and war and the life of princely courts. He received his First Holy Communion from St Charles Borromeo. In the courts he saw ambition, vanity and cruelty, and he chose another master. Against his father's long resistance he gave up his inheritance to his younger brother and entered the Society of Jesus in Rome. There he studied, prayed, and accepted the humblest work. In 1591, when plague and famine struck Rome, he went out with his brother Jesuits to care for the sick, carried a dying man on his shoulders to the hospital, caught the disease, and died on 21 June 1591, aged twenty-three. The heir who could have been first made himself last of all and servant of all. Before he died he wrote to his mother asking her not to grieve for him as for one dead, since he was going to live with God and would help her more from there (Letter to his mother, in substance). The Church has made him a patron of young people and students. As the new school and college year begins in Kerala, let us pray for our students, that they may learn not only to be first in examinations, but to serve.
outline: Opening
Ask: what am I arguing about on the way, and would I be silent if Jesus asked me?
Point 1 · Who is the greatest?
The disciples' silence, and the child placed in the centre.
Point 2 · Whose slave are you?
No neutral ground: our members serve sin or righteousness; wages and gift.
Point 3 · St Aloysius Gonzaga
The heir who chose to be last and servant, and gave his life for the sick.
Take-home line
“Whoever wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all.”
live: Put the least in the centre (Mark 9:36–37)
Notice today the person in your home, class or office who is usually overlooked, and give that person your time and attention.
Present your members to God (Romans 6:19)
Choose one of your members, your eyes, your tongue or your hands, and offer it to God for this week of the fast with one concrete resolution.
2027-06-21.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you came not to be served but to serve, and you placed a little child in the midst of your disciples. Forgive our arguments about who is greatest. Deliver us from the service of sin, which leads to death, and make us slaves of righteousness, that we may receive the gift of eternal life. Through the prayers of St Aloysius Gonzaga, who left the honours of the world to serve you and the sick, give our young people pure hearts and generous hands, and bless all students and teachers in this new school year. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the altar the greatest becomes the least: in the Holy Qurbono the Son of God gives himself under the humble signs of bread and wine, and those who receive him are sent to welcome him in the least of his brothers and sisters.

2027-06-22.title: Tuesday of the fifth week after Pentecost
readings: The one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully: God loves a cheerful giver
Store up treasures in heaven: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also
2027-06-22.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost, in the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu), which ends on 29 June. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today.
2027-06-22.verse: for God loves a cheerful giver.
theo: We are in the middle of the Apostles' Fast, which began last Wednesday and runs to the feast of Sts Peter and Paul. The Church has always kept three companions together in a time of fasting: prayer, fasting and almsgiving. Fasting without prayer becomes a diet; fasting without almsgiving can turn into a private achievement. Today's readings speak of the third companion. St Paul is gathering a collection among the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, and he does not ask the Corinthians to give out of pity or shame. He reaches for a farmer's picture: “The point is this: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.” In these weeks of the monsoon, the paddy fields of Kuttanad and the hill farms of the high ranges are being sown. No farmer throws a single handful on an acre and hopes for a full harvest. Seed that leaves the hand seems lost for a time in the wet earth; in truth it has only gone ahead to become the harvest.

Then Paul says something about the heart of the giver: “Each of you must give as you have made up your mind, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” God does not need our money. What he wants is a heart that has become like his own, a heart that gives because it is glad to give. And Paul is not afraid of running dry: “And God is able to provide you with every blessing in abundance, so that by always having enough of everything, you may share abundantly in every good work.” The one who gives seed to the sower and bread for food will also keep the generous person supplied, so that the giving can go on. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this chapter, pointed out that Paul calls almsgiving a sowing so that no one should think of it as a loss: the seed seems thrown away, but it returns as a harvest, and the harvest is greater than the seed (Homilies on Second Corinthians, in substance). In the fast we give up a meal or a pleasure; the money and the time we save are meant for someone who has less.

The Gospel goes to the root: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust consume and where thieves break in and steal; but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven.” In the time of Jesus wealth was kept in fine clothes, which moths could eat, and in coins and metal, which rust could spoil, or which a thief could dig through a mud wall to take. Our wealth is kept in bank accounts and gold in a locker, but the question has not changed: what will last? Then comes the sentence that searches every heart: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” St Augustine told his people that the poor are like porters who carry our goods ahead of us to heaven: what we give them is not lost but sent on to the place where we hope to live for ever (Sermon 60, in substance). The Apostles whose fast we keep left their nets and boats and found a treasure that no moth could touch. Let us ask, during these days of the fast, where our treasure really is, and let one generous act move it a little closer to heaven.
outline: Opening
Ask: if someone looked at how I spend my money and my time, where would they say my heart is?
Point 1 · Sowing bountifully
Paul's farmer: seed given is not lost but becomes a harvest.
Point 2 · A cheerful giver
God loves a heart that gives gladly, and he keeps the generous supplied.
Point 3 · Treasure in heaven
Moth, rust and thieves cannot reach what is given to God and to the poor.
Take-home line
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
live: Sow bountifully (2 Corinthians 9:6)
Set aside what you save by fasting this week, a meal, a snack, a ride, and give it to someone in need before 29 June.
Move your treasure (Matthew 6:21)
Look honestly at your spending this month and choose one thing to give up so that you can give more.
2027-06-22.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you became poor for our sake so that by your poverty we might become rich. In this Apostles' Fast teach us to sow bountifully and to give with a glad heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion. Take from us the fear that makes us hold on to what moth and rust will consume, and set our hearts on the treasure that is kept in heaven. Bless the hands that give and the hands that receive, and supply us with all we need, so that we may share abundantly in every good work. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the gifts of bread and wine, fruit of the earth and of human work, are brought to the altar, and the Lord returns them to us as his own Body and Blood: the smallest gift placed in his hands becomes a harvest beyond measure.

2027-06-23.title: Wednesday of the fifth week after Pentecost
readings: Tychicus, a dear brother and faithful minister, sent to encourage your hearts
“Lord, I believe”: the man born blind sees, and those who say “We see” remain blind
2027-06-23.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost, in the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu), which ends on 29 June. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. Tomorrow the Church keeps the Birth of John the Baptist.
2027-06-23.verse: He said, “Lord, I believe.” And he worshiped him.
theo: Today we hear the last lines of St Paul's Letter to the Ephesians, and they are not about doctrine but about a friend. “So that you also may know how I am and what I am doing, Tychicus will tell you everything. He is a dear brother and a faithful minister in the Lord. I am sending him to you for this very purpose, to let you know how we are, and to encourage your hearts.” Tychicus is one of those names we pass over quickly. He carried Paul's letters over sea and road, he brought news from the prison, and he sat with the believers to strengthen them. He was not one of the Twelve, and no great church is named after him, yet the Church would not have grown without people like him. The Apostles' Fast honours the Apostles, and with them all the quiet helpers of the gospel: the catechist who teaches on Sunday mornings, the sacristan who opens the church in the rain, the friend who visits the sick. Paul's blessing reaches all of them: “Peace be to the whole community, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Grace be with all who have an undying love for our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Gospel brings us to the end of the long story of the man born blind. Jesus had made mud, anointed his eyes and sent him to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he came back seeing. Instead of rejoicing, his questioners argued, his parents grew afraid, and in the end he was driven out. Then comes a beautiful line: “Jesus heard that they had driven him out, and when he found him, he said, ‘Do you believe in the Son of Man?’” The one whom others pushed out, Jesus goes looking for. The man answers with an open heart: “And who is he, sir? Tell me, so that I may believe in him.” Jesus said to him, “You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” And the man's eyes, which had first seen the light of day, now see the Lord: “Lord, I believe.” And he worshiped him. Through the chapter his faith has grown step by step: he first spoke of “the man called Jesus”, then called him a prophet, then said he must be from God, and now he kneels. St Augustine saw in this man a picture of the catechumen: anointed, sent to the water, washed, and given sight, so that he could worship (Tractates on John 44, in substance). The early Church called Baptism illumination, as St Justin Martyr records (First Apology 61), and every baptized Christian is that man, given eyes to see the Lord.

The last verses turn the light on another kind of blindness. “I came into this world for judgment so that those who do not see may see, and those who do see may become blind.” Some of the Pharisees near him heard this and said to him, “Surely we are not blind, are we?” Jesus said to them, “If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains.” This is not a judgement on a whole people; the evangelist is showing a danger that lives in every religious heart, including ours. The person who knows he is blind can be healed; the person who insists that he sees everything clearly shuts the door on the doctor. A fast is a good time to admit what we cannot see: our own faults, the needs of others at our own table, the hand of God in a hard year. Tomorrow we keep the birth of John the Baptist, who would one day say of Jesus that he must increase. To say “Lord, I believe”, and to kneel, is the beginning of that decrease, and the beginning of true sight.
outline: Opening
Ask: where am I sure that I see clearly, and where might I be blind?
Point 1 · A faithful minister
Tychicus, the quiet helper sent to encourage hearts.
Point 2 · “Lord, I believe”
The man driven out is found by Jesus, and his faith grows into worship.
Point 3 · “We see”
The blindness that will not admit it is blind.
Take-home line
“Lord, I believe.”
live: Encourage one heart (Ephesians 6:22)
Like Tychicus, visit or call one person this week who needs encouragement, and bring them good news.
Admit your blindness (John 9:41)
Before you sleep, ask the Lord to show you one fault you have refused to see, and bring it to confession.
2027-06-23.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, light of the world, you went looking for the man whom others had driven out, and you opened the eyes of his heart to know you. Find us when we are pushed aside, and lead us from faith to worship. Take from us the pride that says “We see” and keeps us blind. Bless all the quiet ministers of your gospel, like Tychicus, who carry your word and encourage hearts. Grant us an undying love for you, and peace to our whole community. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
